meta.blurb: The Count is a perfect host, but every door in his castle is locked, and he casts no reflection in the mirror. Jonathan Harker escapes. Then the Count sails for England, and Jonathan, Mina and a few friends must stop him.
meta.bible: Jonathan Harker: a young English solicitor sent to Transylvania; brave and honest. Mina Murray: Jonathan's fiancée and later wife, a clever schoolteacher who keeps a journal and learns to type. Lucy Westenra: Mina's lively friend, loved by three men. Arthur Holmwood: Lucy's fiancé, later Lord Godalming. Dr John Seward: a young doctor who runs a hospital for troubled minds next to Carfax. Quincey Morris: a brave American from Texas. Professor Abraham Van Helsing: a Dutch doctor and scholar who knows about vampires. Count Dracula: an ancient nobleman who lives in a castle in Transylvania; a vampire, with no reflection, who sleeps in boxes of earth and fears garlic, holy symbols and sunlight. Renfield: a patient in Dr Seward's hospital who eats flies and spiders and serves the Count. Mr Hawkins: Jonathan's employer, an English solicitor. The three women: vampire women who live in the castle. Carfax: an old house in Purfleet, near London, bought by the Count. Whitby: a seaside town in Yorkshire where Lucy and Mina stay. Demeter: the Russian ship that carries the Count to Whitby. Czarina Catherine: the ship that carries him back to Varna. Transylvania: a land in the Carpathian mountains. Bistritz, Borgo Pass, Varna, Galatz, Budapest: places on the way. Piccadilly, Purfleet, London: places in England. Mr Hawkins lives in Exeter and is a kind old man who dies and leaves his fortune to Jonathan and Mina. Munich, Vienna, Buda-Pesth and Klausenburg: stops on Jonathan's journey east; the Golden Krone Hotel stands in Bistritz and its landlord's wife gives Jonathan a small cross on the eve of St George's Day. Szgany and Slovaks: the carters who carry the Count's boxes; a Slovak carter is one of them. The three women are the Count's brides; one is fair and two are dark. Hillingham: Lucy's mother's house in London; Mrs Westenra is Lucy's mother, who has a weak heart. Mr Swales: an old sailor who sits on a seat in the churchyard at Whitby. East Cliff, St Mary's churchyard and the abbey ruins: places in Whitby. Demeter: the Russian schooner wrecked at Whitby with its dead captain tied to the wheel; a huge dog leaps ashore. Sister Agatha: the nurse in Budapest who writes to Mina about Jonathan; the hospital of Saint Joseph and Saint Mary. Bersicker: a wolf that escapes from the zoo and breaks Lucy's window. Amsterdam: where Van Helsing lives. Kingstead: where Lucy is buried. Hampstead: the park where children meet the lady in white. Lord Godalming is Arthur's title after his father dies; his terrier dogs chase the rats at Carfax. Mile End, Bermondsey and Piccadilly: places in London where the Count hid boxes of earth; the Piccadilly house is number 347. Jonathan carries a long curved knife called a kukri; Quincey carries a big bowie knife. Orient Express: the train to Varna. Galatz: a port on the river Danube. Sereth: the river the Count's boat goes up. Hildesheim: the agent at Galatz. Draculas: the Count's family, brave soldiers against the Turks; Szekelys: the people he says he comes from; Attila: a famous leader. Fifty boxes of earth: the Count has them shipped to England, and the friends find twenty-nine of them at Carfax. The sacred wafer is holy bread that the friends use to make the boxes unfit for the Count. Voice and tone: dark, tense and exciting, told through journals and letters; deaths are stated plainly with no gore; fear is built from shadows and strange details; the ending is brave and warm, with the monster destroyed.
chapters: The Beautiful Lady in the Park

beats.scene: Jonathan waves goodbye to Mina at a railway station in London
beats.summary: Jonathan Harker, a young solicitor, leaves Mina and sets out by train to visit Count Dracula for his employer.

beats.scene: A steam train rushes across a wide plain toward a faraway city
beats.summary: Jonathan travels east through Munich and Vienna and sees Buda-Pesth from the train window.

beats.scene: Jonathan writes in a small notebook at a table with a red stew
beats.summary: At a station dinner Jonathan eats chicken with red pepper and writes down the dish for Mina.

beats.scene: Jonathan reads a guidebook as the train climbs a green hillside
beats.summary: In Transylvania Jonathan reads that the mountain people hold many strange old beliefs.

beats.scene: A hotel sign with a golden crown hangs over a street in Bistritz
beats.summary: At the Golden Krone Hotel in Bistritz a letter from the Count waits for Jonathan.

beats.scene: A landlord and his wife whisper in a doorway and shake their heads
beats.summary: The landlord and his wife grow afraid when Jonathan names the castle, and they will say nothing more.

beats.scene: An old woman clasps her hands and begs a young man at an inn
beats.summary: The old woman begs Jonathan not to go, since the eve of St George's Day is a night of evil.

beats.scene: Jonathan fastens a small cross around his neck beside a narrow bed
beats.summary: Jonathan accepts the cross to be polite, and that night he dreams of howling dogs.

beats.scene: Peasants crowd round a yellow coach and point two fingers at Jonathan
beats.summary: Next morning the peasants cross themselves and point two fingers at him, and the guidebook explains their strange words.

beats.scene: A coach climbs a green hillside toward dark mountains at sunset
beats.summary: The coach rolls through orchards and woods toward the Borgo Pass while the driver whips the horses on.

beats.scene: A coach stops at a windy mountain pass as the light fades
beats.summary: At the Borgo Pass the coachman halts, and there is no carriage waiting for Jonathan.

beats.scene: Four black horses and a tall driver wait on a dark mountain road
beats.summary: A carriage drawn by four black horses arrives, driven by a tall man with a long beard and glowing eyes.

beats.scene: The black carriage speeds along a road between dark pine trees
beats.summary: Jonathan changes coaches, and the driver sets off at great speed into the night.

beats.scene: Jonathan looks out at a silent road under a cold moon as dogs howl
beats.summary: The road seems to run in circles, dogs howl in the dark, and the driver whispers that the dead travel fast.

beats.scene: A small blue flame flickers beside the road as a driver steps down
beats.summary: Pale blue flames flicker beside the road, and the driver stops to look at one.

beats.scene: Grey wolves circle the carriage in the moonlight as horses shiver
beats.summary: Wolves gather around the carriage, until the driver raises his arm and they melt away.

beats.scene: A black carriage rolls into a stone courtyard beneath huge broken walls
beats.summary: The carriage enters the courtyard of a vast ruined castle, and the driver lifts down Jonathan's bag.

beats.scene: Jonathan stands alone in a dark courtyard before a great carved door
beats.summary: Jonathan waits in the cold courtyard, afraid that this is a dream, until he hears footsteps.

beats.scene: A tall old man in black holds a lamp in an open castle doorway
beats.summary: Count Dracula opens the door and bids Jonathan enter freely, and his hand is as cold as ice.

beats.scene: Count Dracula leads Jonathan upstairs to a warm room with a fire and supper
beats.summary: The Count carries Jonathan's bags upstairs and shows him a warm room where supper is waiting.

beats.scene: Jonathan lathers his face before a small mirror hung on a sunny window
beats.summary: Jonathan wakes late and begins to shave with a small mirror hung on the window.

beats.scene: A razor stops in mid-air as a mirror shows an empty room behind
beats.summary: A voice behind Jonathan says good morning, he cuts himself, and the mirror shows no reflection of the Count.

beats.scene: A mirror falls from a high castle window to a stone courtyard
beats.summary: The Count reaches for Jonathan's throat, draws back from the cross, and throws the mirror out of the window.

beats.scene: Bread and cheese stand on an empty table in a bright room
beats.summary: Jonathan finds breakfast laid, sees no servants, and realises that the Count never eats or drinks.

beats.scene: Jonathan reads a book in a library full of English newspapers and maps
beats.summary: Jonathan finds a library of English books and magazines that the Count has studied for years.

beats.scene: The Count sits by a lamp, pale and tall, with white teeth
beats.summary: At night the Count asks Jonathan to correct his English, and Jonathan studies his strange face.

beats.scene: The Count and Jonathan lean over law books in the lamplight
beats.summary: The Count questions Jonathan about English law, solicitors and the shipping of goods.

beats.scene: Jonathan unrolls the plan of an old house with a chapel and a pond
beats.summary: Jonathan describes the house at Carfax, and the Count says he likes it because it is old and dark.

beats.scene: The Count stands proudly beside a coat of arms and an old battle painting
beats.summary: The Count tells the proud history of his people, the Szekelys, who fought the Turks.

beats.scene: The Count turns his head sharply at the sound of a distant cock crowing
beats.summary: At the first cock-crow of dawn the Count stops talking and leaves the room quickly.

beats.scene: Two men sit by a fire as one hands over a folded letter
beats.summary: The Count asks Jonathan to stay a whole month and to write to Mr Hawkins about it.

beats.scene: A tall man raises one finger in a candle-lit stone corridor
beats.summary: The Count warns Jonathan never to sleep in any room of the castle except his own.

beats.scene: A great door stands open on a dark night as wolves howl outside
beats.summary: Jonathan says he wants to go home, but the Count opens the door on a night full of wolves.

beats.scene: Jonathan shakes a heavy iron door handle in a long stone hallway
beats.summary: Jonathan tries every door in the castle, finds them all locked, and understands that he is a prisoner.

beats.scene: Jonathan writes at a desk while the Count waits with three sheets of paper
beats.summary: The Count makes Jonathan write three letters dated for later weeks, so that no one will worry about him.

beats.scene: A man in black crawls head first down a castle wall above a valley
beats.summary: From his window Jonathan sees the Count crawling down the castle wall like a lizard.

beats.scene: Jonathan opens a heavy door into a quiet moonlit room with old furniture
beats.summary: Jonathan breaks the Count's warning and falls asleep in a quiet room in another part of the castle.

beats.scene: Three pale women with red lips stand in moonlight over a sleeping man
beats.summary: Jonathan wakes to find three strange women in the room who want to kiss him.

beats.scene: A tall man in black flings out his arm in fury, moonlit room
beats.summary: The Count rushes in, drives the women back, and says that Jonathan belongs to him.

beats.scene: The Count holds out a moving sack to three women in a dark room
beats.summary: The Count gives the women a bag that cries like a child, and Jonathan faints.

beats.scene: Jonathan sits up in bed beside neatly folded clothes on a chair
beats.summary: Jonathan wakes in his own bed with his clothes folded beside him, and knows that the Count carried him there.

beats.scene: A man in a borrowed brown suit walks out of a castle gate
beats.summary: The Count leaves the castle dressed in Jonathan's own clothes, so that the villagers will blame Jonathan for his crimes.

beats.scene: A woman beats on a castle gate while grey wolves run from the forest
beats.summary: A woman begs the Count at the gate for her child, and the wolves silence her cries.

beats.scene: Jonathan stands in a dusty bare room beside a great heap of gold
beats.summary: In the Count's bare room Jonathan finds a heap of old gold and a heavy door in the corner.

beats.scene: Jonathan carries a candle down a narrow winding stair under the castle
beats.summary: Jonathan follows a stair and a tunnel down toward the smell of fresh earth.

beats.scene: Rows of big wooden boxes stand in a ruined chapel among broken tombs
beats.summary: In an old ruined chapel Jonathan finds many boxes filled with fresh earth.

beats.scene: The Count lies pale and still in a wooden box of earth
beats.summary: In one box lies the Count, still and cold like a dead man, but with a fuller, younger face.

beats.scene: Jonathan swings a spade at a pale face as red eyes glare at him
beats.summary: Jonathan strikes at the Count with a spade, but the staring eyes freeze him, and he runs.

beats.scene: Men with ropes and hammers nail the lids of boxes beside a loaded cart
beats.summary: The Szgany nail down the boxes and load them onto carts, and then they drive away from the castle.

beats.scene: Jonathan climbs out of a high castle window onto a sheer wall at night
beats.summary: Jonathan writes a last goodbye to Mina and climbs out of the window to try to reach freedom.

beats.scene: Mina sits at a school desk beside a typewriter and an open letter
beats.summary: Mina Murray teaches at a school in Exeter and learns shorthand and typing to help Jonathan.

beats.scene: Lucy laughs as she writes a long letter at a garden table
beats.summary: Lucy writes to Mina that three men have asked her to marry them in one day.

beats.scene: Dr Seward bows politely to Lucy in a sunny drawing room
beats.summary: Dr John Seward asks Lucy to marry him, and she kindly refuses.

beats.scene: A tall cheerful American in a travelling coat shakes Lucy's hand
beats.summary: Quincey Morris of Texas asks next and is refused, but he promises to stay her friend.

beats.scene: Lucy weeps and smiles as a young man kneels before her
beats.summary: Lucy accepts Arthur Holmwood, the man she loves, with tears of joy.

beats.scene: Dr Seward speaks into a phonograph at a lamp-lit desk in his study
beats.summary: Sad and busy, Dr Seward keeps his diary on a phonograph at his hospital next to Carfax.

beats.scene: A strong grey-haired patient sits calmly in a plain room with a barred window
beats.summary: Dr Seward studies a patient called Renfield, a polite and clever man with a strange habit.

beats.scene: A patient in a bare room holds a fly beside a small box
beats.summary: Renfield catches and eats flies, then spiders, then sparrows, hoping to gain their life.

beats.scene: Three men raise glasses in a warm room under a lamp
beats.summary: That night Quincey, Seward and Arthur drink to Lucy's health and promise to stay friends.

beats.scene: Mina folds a letter beside a packed trunk in a small bedroom
beats.summary: With no word from Jonathan, Mina accepts Lucy's invitation to stay at Whitby.

beats.scene: Two young women hug on a sunny railway platform beside a gentle older woman
beats.summary: Mina arrives at Whitby, and Lucy and her mother meet her at the station.

beats.scene: Red roofs climb a hillside above a busy harbour and a ruined abbey
beats.summary: Mina describes the old town of Whitby, its harbour, its river and the abbey on the cliff.

beats.scene: Two friends sit on a seat among old gravestones above a wide grey sea
beats.summary: Mina and Lucy climb to the churchyard on the cliff and make a seat there their favourite place.

beats.scene: An old white-bearded sailor in a thick coat points at a gravestone
beats.summary: On the seat they meet Mr Swales, an old sailor, who says the gravestones tell lies.

beats.scene: An old sailor laughs beside a stone cross as the sea shines below
beats.summary: Mr Swales says he is over ninety and does not fear death, and the sea has taken many of his friends.

beats.scene: Mina writes in a journal by lamplight at an open window
beats.summary: Mina writes in her journal and worries that she has heard nothing from Jonathan.

beats.scene: Mina ties a small key to her wrist beside Lucy's sleeping bed
beats.summary: Mrs Westenra says Lucy walked in her sleep as a child, so Mina locks the door and ties the key to her wrist.

beats.scene: Lucy blushes and smiles over a letter at a breakfast table by a window
beats.summary: A letter from Arthur says that his father is ill and that he cannot come to Whitby yet.

beats.scene: A still grey sea lies under a heavy sky as old sailors look up
beats.summary: The weather turns hot and strangely still, and the old sailors say they do not like the look of it.

beats.scene: A blood-red sunset glows above crowded fishing boats entering a harbour
beats.summary: At sunset the sky turns red, the boats hurry in, and the coastguard warns that a great storm is coming.

beats.scene: Huge grey waves crash over a harbour wall as people crowd on a cliff
beats.summary: A great storm breaks over Whitby, and half the town gathers on the cliff to watch the sea.

beats.scene: A schooner under full sail races through lightning toward a harbour mouth
beats.summary: A Russian schooner, the Demeter, races toward the harbour with a motionless man at the wheel.

beats.scene: A wrecked ship with torn sails lies on a beach beneath a high cliff
beats.summary: The ship drives onto the sand beneath the East Cliff with a tremendous crash.

beats.scene: A huge dog bounds from a stranded ship onto the beach in the dark
beats.summary: A huge dog leaps from the deck, runs up the cliff to the churchyard and disappears.

beats.scene: A lantern shines on a dead man tied to the wheel of a ship
beats.summary: The coastguard finds the captain dead at the wheel, his hands tied to it and a crucifix wound in his fingers.

beats.scene: A sealed bottle with a rolled paper lies in a man's coat pocket
beats.summary: The captain's log is found, and it tells of a cargo of fifty boxes of earth sent from Varna.

beats.scene: A tall thin shadow stands on a ship's dark deck beside a frightened sailor
beats.summary: The log says that the crew vanished one by one and that the mate saw a tall thin stranger.

beats.scene: An old captain ties his hands to a ship's wheel in a roaring storm
beats.summary: The mate jumps overboard, and the captain ties himself to the wheel to steer to harbour.

beats.scene: A long line of people follows a coffin up a stone stair
beats.summary: The whole town follows the captain's coffin to the churchyard and honours him as a hero.

beats.scene: An old sailor lies back stiffly on a seat in a morning churchyard
beats.summary: Old Mr Swales is found dead on his favourite seat in the churchyard, his neck broken.

beats.scene: Mina sits up in a dark bedroom beside an empty moonlit bed
beats.summary: In the night Mina wakes and finds that Lucy is gone from her bed.

beats.scene: A girl in white sits as a dark shape bends over her
beats.summary: Mina runs to the cliff and sees Lucy on the seat with a long dark shape bending over her.

beats.scene: Mina pins a shawl around the throat of a sleeping girl on a seat
beats.summary: The dark shape is gone, and Lucy has two small red marks on her throat.

beats.scene: Lucy sits pale at a breakfast table in the morning light
beats.summary: Lucy remembers nothing of the night except a strange dream, and she is paler than before.

beats.scene: Mina reads a letter from a nun in a sunny window with trembling hands
beats.summary: A letter arrives from Sister Agatha in Budapest, saying that Jonathan is alive and very ill.

beats.scene: Mina packs a small bag as a train waits steaming at a station
beats.summary: Mina leaves Lucy with her mother and takes the first train across Europe to Budapest.

beats.scene: A thin pale man in a hospital bed opens his arms to Mina
beats.summary: In the hospital Jonathan, thin and much older, knows Mina at once.

beats.scene: Mina ties a small book with ribbon and presses red wax on it
beats.summary: Jonathan gives Mina his shorthand journal and asks her not to read it unless duty demands.

beats.scene: A bride and groom hold hands in a plain hospital chapel beside a nun
beats.summary: Jonathan and Mina marry in the hospital chapel, with Sister Agatha as a witness.

beats.scene: An old man opens a country house door to welcome a young couple
beats.summary: Back in Exeter Mr Hawkins welcomes them, and Jonathan slowly recovers his strength.

beats.scene: A big bat flaps against a window above a pale girl in a bed
beats.summary: Back in London Lucy sleeps badly, hears a bat at her window at night, and grows pale.

beats.scene: A worried young man writes a letter beside a sick old man's bed
beats.summary: Arthur cannot leave his sick father, so he asks his friend Dr Seward to examine Lucy.

beats.scene: A young doctor holds a thin pale girl's wrist and listens
beats.summary: Dr Seward finds Lucy thin and bloodless but cannot find any illness to explain it.

beats.scene: A doctor writes a telegram at his desk by lamplight
beats.summary: Puzzled, Dr Seward sends for his old teacher, Professor Van Helsing of Amsterdam.

beats.scene: A short broad man with grey hair looks closely at a girl's throat
beats.summary: Van Helsing examines Lucy, sees the two small marks on her throat, and grows grave.

beats.scene: A young man lies beside a girl while a tube joins their arms
beats.summary: Van Helsing performs a blood transfusion, and Arthur is the first to give Lucy his blood.

beats.scene: A white wreath of garlic flowers hangs on a window beside a sleeping girl
beats.summary: Van Helsing fills Lucy's room with garlic flowers and puts a wreath around her neck.

beats.scene: A tired young doctor gives blood through a tube beside a bed
beats.summary: On the second night Dr Seward gives his own blood to Lucy.

beats.scene: An old professor holds out his arm in lamplight as a girl sleeps
beats.summary: On the third night Van Helsing gives his own blood, and Lucy sleeps without bad dreams.

beats.scene: A tall American in a travelling coat rolls up his sleeve beside a bed
beats.summary: Quincey Morris arrives, gives his blood too, and the men watch hopefully over Lucy.

beats.scene: An old professor gives strict orders to a young doctor at a door
beats.summary: Van Helsing must go to Amsterdam, and he tells Seward to guard Lucy and keep the garlic and shut windows.

beats.scene: A kind old woman carries garlic flowers out of a bedroom to the window
beats.summary: Lucy's mother dislikes the smell, takes the garlic away and opens the window, and Lucy weakens.

beats.scene: A young doctor reads a telegram in a bright morning room too late
beats.summary: Tired, Seward goes home to rest for one night, and Van Helsing's warning telegram reaches him too late.

beats.scene: Mother and daughter lie in one big bed as wings flap outside
beats.summary: Lucy and her mother lie in the same bed, and Lucy hears wings at the window and a wolf far away.

beats.scene: A huge grey wolf thrusts its head through shattered glass in a bedroom window
beats.summary: A huge wolf, escaped from the zoo, breaks the window glass.

beats.scene: A kind old woman falls across a bed as a wolf stares in
beats.summary: Lucy's mother sees the wolf and dies of fright, her weak heart unable to bear it.

beats.scene: A weak girl lies under her mother's body in a dark cold room
beats.summary: Lucy lies helpless and calls for the servants, who are in a deep and unnatural sleep.

beats.scene: A doctor stands horrified in a morning bedroom with a broken window
beats.summary: Seward finds the broken window and Lucy near death, and Van Helsing hurries back with fresh garlic.

beats.scene: A pale girl reaches for a young man as an old man pulls him
beats.summary: Lucy asks Arthur for a kiss, but Van Helsing pulls him away, afraid of what he sees in her face.

beats.scene: Three men stand beside a bed where a beautiful pale girl lies still
beats.summary: Lucy dies, and her face grows soft and beautiful, while Van Helsing wonders whether it is the end.

beats.scene: Mourners stand in grey wind beside an open stone tomb in a village churchyard
beats.summary: Lucy is buried in the family tomb at Kingstead, and Van Helsing watches the tomb with a worried face.

beats.scene: A newspaper lies on a table beside a small child's shoe
beats.summary: Newspapers report children lost on the heath at night, each with two small throat wounds, who talk of a beautiful lady.

beats.scene: Two doctors stand beside a small child's hospital bed in a dim ward
beats.summary: Van Helsing shows Seward a child with wounds like Lucy's and tells him that some dead do not rest.

beats.scene: Two men with lanterns lean over an empty lead coffin in a dark vault
beats.summary: At night Van Helsing and Seward open Lucy's coffin and find it empty.

beats.scene: A white figure carrying a child glides between dark yew trees in a churchyard
beats.summary: They hide among the yew trees, and a white lady with a child in her arms comes toward the tomb.

beats.scene: A woman in white shrinks back from a raised golden cross in lantern light
beats.summary: Van Helsing's lantern shows Lucy's cruel face, and she is driven back by his cross.

beats.scene: An angry young man faces an old professor in a lamplit study
beats.summary: Next day Van Helsing tells Arthur and Quincey the truth, and Arthur is angry, then convinced.

beats.scene: Four men with lanterns lean over a coffin holding a beautiful sleeping woman
beats.summary: That night the four men open the coffin, and Lucy lies there lovely, with red lips and sharp teeth.

beats.scene: An old professor hands a wooden stake and hammer to a pale young man
beats.summary: Van Helsing says only a stake can free Lucy, and Arthur says that he will do it himself.

beats.scene: Four men walk out of a stone tomb into the grey light of dawn
beats.summary: Arthur drives the stake, Lucy rests in peace, and Van Helsing says that the one who made her is still free.

beats.scene: A young couple in black stand beside an old man's grave
beats.summary: Old Mr Hawkins dies suddenly and leaves his fortune to Jonathan and Mina.

beats.scene: A young couple walk arm in arm past bright shop windows in London
beats.summary: Jonathan and Mina move to London, and one afternoon they walk along Piccadilly.

beats.scene: A tall thin man with a pointed beard stares at a pretty girl
beats.summary: Jonathan stops, white-faced, as a tall man with a pointed beard stares at a girl across the street.

beats.scene: A tall man glares from a cab window at a shaking young man
beats.summary: Jonathan whispers that the man is the Count grown young, and the Count drives away with a look of hatred.

beats.scene: Mina breaks a wax seal on a small book beside a sleeping man
beats.summary: That night Mina decides that the solemn duty has come, and she opens Jonathan's journal.

beats.scene: Mina sits up reading a thick journal as dawn grows grey in a window
beats.summary: Mina reads all night and understands that the terrible story is true.

beats.scene: Two people hold each other beside a breakfast table in the morning sun
beats.summary: Mina tells Jonathan that she believes every word, and he weeps with relief.

beats.scene: Mina holds a telegram beside a teapot in a small sunny room
beats.summary: A telegram says that Professor Van Helsing wishes to meet Mina.

beats.scene: A grey-haired professor sits reading papers at a table as a young couple wait
beats.summary: Van Helsing arrives and reads Mina's diary and Jonathan's journal for hours.

beats.scene: A professor shakes the hand of a pale young man with shining eyes
beats.summary: Van Helsing thanks Jonathan, says the journal explains everything, and invites them to join the friends at Purfleet.

beats.scene: A young couple walk up a path to a grey hospital behind a wall
beats.summary: Jonathan and Mina arrive at Dr Seward's hospital at Purfleet, and Jonathan sees Carfax beyond the wall.

beats.scene: Mina sits at a typewriter beside a phonograph as a tear falls
beats.summary: Mina offers to type Dr Seward's phonograph diary and learns what happened to Lucy.

beats.scene: Six people sit round a table covered with neat typed pages
beats.summary: Arthur and Quincey arrive, and the whole company gathers around Mina's typed pages.

beats.scene: A grey-haired professor stands and speaks to five listeners in a study
beats.summary: Van Helsing tells them that Dracula is a vampire as strong as twenty men who commands wolves, bats and fog.

beats.scene: A cross and a string of garlic lie beside a lamp on a table
beats.summary: Van Helsing lists the vampire's weaknesses: garlic, holy things, an invitation, and the light of day.

beats.scene: A professor points to a map of London marked with small crosses
beats.summary: Van Helsing proposes finding every box of earth and making it unfit for the Count.

beats.scene: A young man opens a ledger of delivery papers on a study desk
beats.summary: Jonathan explains how the fifty boxes came by sea to Whitby and then to Carfax.

beats.scene: A doctor points from an upstairs window at an old house behind a wall
beats.summary: Dr Seward shows them Carfax from an upstairs window, close beside his hospital.

beats.scene: A gentle young woman stands in a plain room before a bowing grey-haired patient
beats.summary: Mina meets Renfield, who is calm and polite and looks strangely sad.

beats.scene: A patient kneels in a bare cell as a doctor shakes his head
beats.summary: Renfield begs Dr Seward to set him free, but the doctor refuses.

beats.scene: Five men carry lanterns across dark grass toward a dim old house
beats.summary: Five men set out for Carfax at night with lanterns, keys and holy things, while Mina watches from the hospital.

beats.scene: A man turns a rusty key in a great old door at night
beats.summary: Jonathan unlocks the old front door, and a smell of damp earth comes out.

beats.scene: Lantern light shows dusty rooms with thick spider webs in a long hall
beats.summary: The men search the dusty rooms of Carfax in silence.

beats.scene: Rows of big wooden boxes stand in an old stone chapel in lantern light
beats.summary: In the old chapel the friends count twenty-nine boxes of earth, though fifty came to England.

beats.scene: Hundreds of rats with shining eyes pour across the stone floor of a chapel
beats.summary: Hundreds of huge rats rush into the chapel from every corner.

beats.scene: Three small dogs chase grey rats across stone floors as a man whistles
beats.summary: Arthur whistles, his terriers rush in, and the rats flee.

beats.scene: An old professor lays a small white wafer inside an open box of earth
beats.summary: Van Helsing places holy bread in each box so that the Count can never rest in it.

beats.scene: A young man holds up a bundle of labelled keys and papers
beats.summary: In the study Jonathan finds keys and deeds for other houses in Piccadilly, Mile End and Bermondsey.

beats.scene: A clerk and a young man bend over a dusty ledger
beats.summary: At the carriers' office Jonathan learns that the missing boxes were taken to those three houses.

beats.scene: A young woman at a typewriter looks sadly at men talking by a window
beats.summary: The men decide to keep Mina away from danger, and she waits sadly at the hospital.

beats.scene: A patient in white runs across dark grass toward a wall as nurses chase
beats.summary: Renfield escapes through an open door and runs toward Carfax, with Dr Seward and two nurses chasing him.

beats.scene: A patient stands under a dark chapel window, speaking to nobody
beats.summary: Seward finds Renfield outside Carfax, talking to an unseen master.

beats.scene: A huge bat flies over three men holding a struggling man at night
beats.summary: A huge bat flies over them, and Renfield cries out that he serves the master.

beats.scene: A patient sits quietly on a narrow bed as a doctor writes
beats.summary: Back in his room Renfield falls silent, and Seward does not understand him.

beats.scene: A pale young woman rubs her eyes at a window beside a sleeping man
beats.summary: Mina and Jonathan begin to sleep too deeply, and Mina grows tired and pale.

beats.scene: White mist creeps under a bedroom door as two red eyes shine
beats.summary: Mina dreams of a white mist and two red eyes in her room.

beats.scene: A smiling patient shakes a doctor's hand and then bows his head
beats.summary: Renfield is calm and cheerful by day, then begs to be sent far away from Purfleet.

beats.scene: A doctor runs along a dark corridor with a lamp at night
beats.summary: In the night Seward hears a cry and a fall from Renfield's room.

beats.scene: A badly hurt patient whispers to a kneeling doctor on a cell floor
beats.summary: Renfield tells the doctors that the master has gone to Mrs Harker, and then he dies.

beats.scene: Four men crash against a locked bedroom door in a hospital hallway
beats.summary: The four men run to Mina's room and break down the locked door.

beats.scene: A tall man in black holds a kneeling woman beside a sleeping man
beats.summary: The friends burst in and see the Count holding Mina against his chest while Jonathan lies in a stupor.

beats.scene: A man in black turns to white mist before a professor's white wafer
beats.summary: Van Helsing holds up the holy bread, and the Count turns into mist and escapes.

beats.scene: A kneeling woman covers her face as an old man touches her brow
beats.summary: Mina cries that she is unclean, and the holy bread leaves a red scar on her forehead.

beats.scene: A young man with white hair weeps beside his wife in grey morning light
beats.summary: Jonathan wakes, and by morning his hair has turned white with grief.

beats.scene: Mina sits wrapped in a shawl and tells her story to five pale listeners
beats.summary: Mina tells her friends what the Count did and what he said to her.

beats.scene: Five hands rest on one another in a lamplit study as a woman watches
beats.summary: Mina asks the men to promise to free her if she ever becomes a vampire, and they swear.

beats.scene: An old professor speaks gently to a pale woman with a red forehead mark
beats.summary: Van Helsing says Mina can now sometimes feel the Count, which is a danger and also a weapon.

beats.scene: Six people sit round a table in morning light with open notebooks
beats.summary: The men promise there will be no more secrets, and Mina joins the band.

beats.scene: Friends in dark coats stand before the door of a tall empty house
beats.summary: The friends go to the Count's empty house in Piccadilly, and Jonathan opens the door with his key.

beats.scene: Open wooden boxes of earth stand in a row in a dusty back room
beats.summary: In a back room they find the Count's boxes, and a key turns in the front door.

beats.scene: A tall pale man enters a dusty hall; a young man draws a knife
beats.summary: Count Dracula walks into the Piccadilly house, and Jonathan springs at him with his long curved knife.

beats.scene: A torn black coat spills gold coins across a dusty floor
beats.summary: The knife cuts the Count's coat, and a rain of gold coins and papers falls to the floor.

beats.scene: A man in black dives through a window in a shower of broken glass
beats.summary: The Count dives out of the window into the yard below.

beats.scene: A pale man smiles cruelly in a stable yard beneath a broken window
beats.summary: The Count says from the yard that his revenge has only begun, and he vanishes.

beats.scene: A young man lays white wafers in boxes of earth in a cellar
beats.summary: The friends treat the boxes at the houses in Mile End and Bermondsey, leaving the Count one fewer hiding place.

beats.scene: A woman sleeps upright in a chair as an old professor raises a hand
beats.summary: At sunrise Van Helsing sends Mina into a trance, and she hears water lapping and wood creaking.

beats.scene: An old professor frowns in thought beside a window in grey morning light
beats.summary: Van Helsing understands that the Count is in his box on a ship leaving England.

beats.scene: Dockers load barrels onto a tall ship at a quay as men ask questions
beats.summary: At the docks the friends learn that the Czarina Catherine has sailed for Varna with one strange large box.

beats.scene: A map of Europe on a table with a line toward the Black Sea
beats.summary: Van Helsing says that the Count is going home to his castle, and the friends decide to follow.

beats.scene: A group of travellers with trunks board a steaming train at a London station
beats.summary: Mina insists on going, and the whole group leaves London by train for Varna.

beats.scene: A steaming train pulls into a station beside a blue sea
beats.summary: The friends cross Europe by train and reach Varna on the Black Sea.

beats.scene: A pale woman sits in a trance as an old man waits beside her
beats.summary: Each day Van Helsing puts Mina into a trance, but the ship does not come.

beats.scene: A man holds a telegram at a hotel desk as friends grab coats
beats.summary: A telegram says the ship has been sent to Galatz, so the friends hurry to take a train there.

beats.scene: A ship's captain talks to travellers beside a ship tied at a river quay
beats.summary: At Galatz the captain tells them that a man took the Count's big box away.

beats.scene: Strong men lift a large wooden box onto a boat at a river bank
beats.summary: Slovak carters took the box up the river Sereth on a boat, headed for the mountains.

beats.scene: Three small groups point in three directions on a map by lamplight
beats.summary: The friends split into three groups to follow the boat by river and by road.

beats.scene: A small steam launch speeds up a wide winding river between green hills
beats.summary: Jonathan and Arthur chase the boat up the river in a swift steam launch.

beats.scene: Two riders gallop beside a river with rifles at their saddles
beats.summary: Quincey and Seward ride along the bank, ready if the boat turns toward the shore.

beats.scene: A carriage climbs a rough mountain road carrying an old man and a woman
beats.summary: Van Helsing and Mina travel by road toward the Borgo Pass as Mina senses the Count moving.

beats.scene: A fire burns inside a wide circle in the snow as pale women wait
beats.summary: Van Helsing draws a circle of holy bread around Mina, and three pale women call to her but cannot cross it.

beats.scene: An old professor climbs a snowy path toward a dark castle at dawn
beats.summary: Van Helsing leaves Mina in the safe circle, goes alone to the castle, and frees the three women in their tombs.

beats.scene: A white wafer lies on a great stone tomb inside a gloomy chapel
beats.summary: Van Helsing seals the Count's tomb and the castle doorway so the Count can never rest there again.

beats.scene: A cart with a long box races along a mountain road at sunset
beats.summary: The friends close in from three sides on the Count's cart as the sun sinks.

beats.scene: Two men leap onto a speeding cart with knives raised in red evening light
beats.summary: Jonathan and Quincey leap onto the cart, and their knives end the Count, who crumbles into dust with a look of peace.

beats.scene: A wounded man lies smiling on the ground as friends kneel in snow
beats.summary: Quincey, wounded, tells his friends he is glad to have helped, and he dies as Mina's forehead is clean.

beats.scene: Weary travellers walk down a mountain road away from a ruined castle
beats.summary: The friends leave the mountains grieving for Quincey but thankful that the evil is gone.

beats.scene: A young couple sit in a sunny English garden beside a sleeping baby
beats.summary: Back in England Jonathan and Mina rebuild their lives, and Arthur and Seward marry happily.

beats.scene: A small boy stands between his parents in front of a warm fireplace
beats.summary: Seven years later Jonathan and Mina have a son, born on the day Quincey died, and they call him Quincey.

beats.scene: A family of three stands holding hands before a distant castle on a mountain
beats.summary: That summer the family revisits Transylvania, and the castle stands silent above the quiet valley.

beats.scene: An old professor smiles as he holds a small boy on his knee
beats.summary: Van Helsing says that no proof is needed, and Jonathan writes a final note about the typed papers and his brave wife.

A1A2: Jonathan Harker says goodbye to Mina and takes a train from London.
The train goes through Munich and Vienna, and Jonathan sees many new places.
Jonathan eats chicken with red pepper and writes down how it is made.
Jonathan reads that people in these mountains believe in many strange and scary things.
At the Golden Krone Hotel, a letter from the Count is waiting.
The hotel owner and his wife look afraid when Jonathan speaks about the castle.
The old woman begs him to wait, because tonight is a night when bad things walk.
She gives him a small cross, and Jonathan wears it to make her happy.
In the morning, people around the coach point two fingers and say strange words.
The coach goes up into the hills, and the mountains grow dark ahead.
The coach stops at the Borgo Pass, but nobody is waiting for Jonathan.
Soon a black carriage arrives with four black horses and a very tall driver.
Jonathan changes to the black carriage, and the driver goes very fast.
The road seems to go in circles, and dogs cry out in the dark.
Jonathan sees a small blue light beside the road, and the driver stops.
Wolves come close to the carriage, but the driver raises his arm.
The carriage drives into the yard of a huge old castle.
Jonathan waits alone in the cold yard, and he is very afraid.
A tall old man opens the door, and his hand is cold as ice.
Count Dracula carries the bags up the stairs to a warm room.
Jonathan wakes late in the morning and hangs a small mirror on the window.
Jonathan sees the room in the mirror, but the Count is not there.
The Count reaches for his neck, sees the cross, and pulls back.
Jonathan sees a table with food, but the Count never eats or drinks.
Jonathan finds a big room full of English books, and he reads for hours.
At night the Count asks Jonathan to help with his English.
The Count asks many questions about English law, ships, and how to buy houses.
Carfax is an old house with a chapel, a pond, and a high wall.
The Count says his family are brave soldiers who fought many wars long ago.
At first light, the Count stops talking and quickly leaves the room.
The Count asks Jonathan to stay for a whole month in the castle.
The Count warns Jonathan never to sleep in any room except his own.
Jonathan asks to leave, but outside the open door, many wolves are waiting.
Jonathan tries every door in the castle, and every door is locked.
The Count makes Jonathan write three letters home with dates that are not true.
One night Jonathan sees the Count climb down the castle wall like an insect.
Jonathan finds an open door and goes into a quiet room in the moonlight.
Three beautiful women come into the room, and they want to kiss Jonathan.
The Count rushes in angrily and says that Jonathan belongs to him.
The Count throws the women a bag that moves, and Jonathan faints.
Jonathan wakes in his bed, and his clothes are folded on a chair.
The Count leaves the castle in Jonathan's own clothes and walks into the night.
A woman at the gate cries for her child, but the wolves come.
Jonathan finds the Count's empty room, with old gold in big piles.
Jonathan finds a stair and goes down under the castle with a candle.
In an old chapel, big wooden boxes stand full of fresh dark earth.
In one box the Count lies still like a dead man, with open eyes.
Jonathan swings a spade at him, but the staring eyes make him freeze.
Strong men nail the boxes shut and carry them away on carts.
Jonathan decides to climb down the wall, and he writes goodbye to Mina.
Mina works as a teacher and learns to type to help Jonathan.
Lucy writes a happy letter to Mina and says she has big news.
First, Dr Seward asks Lucy to marry him, and she says no kindly.
Next, Quincey Morris, a tall American, asks too, and she says no again.
Last, Arthur Holmwood asks, and Lucy cries and says yes with a happy heart.
Dr Seward is sad, so he works hard and speaks his diary into a machine.
A patient called Renfield lives at his hospital, and he is strong and strange.
Renfield catches flies and spiders, and he eats them to gain their life.
That night the three men drink together and promise to stay good friends.
Jonathan does not write, so Mina goes to stay with Lucy at Whitby.
Mina arrives at Whitby, and Lucy and her mother meet her at the station.
Whitby has red roofs, a busy harbour, and a ruined abbey on the cliff.
Mina and Lucy climb to the old church, where seats look out over the sea.
An old sailor named Mr Swales says that many old stones tell lies.
Mr Swales is very old, and he laughs when he talks about death.
At night Mina writes in her journal, and she worries because Jonathan is silent.
Mrs Westenra tells Mina that Lucy sometimes walks in her sleep at night.
Lucy gets a letter from Arthur, and she smiles all through the day.
The day is hot and very still, and the sea looks like glass.
At sunset, the sky turns red, and the fishermen hurry their boats home.
A huge storm arrives, and the people of Whitby watch the waves from the cliff.
Out at sea, a ship with all its sails comes rushing toward the harbour.
The ship runs onto the sand under the cliff with a great noise.
A huge dog jumps from the ship and runs up toward the old church.
Men find the captain dead, with his hands tied to the wheel.
The captain's book says the ship came from Varna with boxes of earth.
One by one, the men on the ship disappear, and a tall thin stranger appears.
The captain writes that he is alone, and he ties himself to the wheel.
The whole town walks in a long line to the captain's funeral.
The next morning, someone finds old Mr Swales dead on his seat.
One night, Mina wakes up and sees that Lucy's bed is empty.
Mina runs to the cliff and sees Lucy on the seat with a dark shape.
The shape is gone when Mina arrives, and Lucy has two small red marks.
Mina takes Lucy home, and Lucy does not remember anything the next day.
Sister Agatha writes that Jonathan is alive, but he is very ill.
Jonathan is very ill, so Mina goes to Budapest on the first train.
Jonathan is thin and weak, but he smiles when he sees Mina.
Jonathan gives Mina his journal, and she promises not to read it.
Jonathan and Mina marry in the hospital, and a kind nurse watches.
Back in England, Jonathan slowly grows stronger, and Mr Hawkins welcomes them kindly.
Lucy goes home to London, but she sleeps badly and grows pale.
Arthur is worried about Lucy, so he asks his friend Dr Seward to help.
Dr Seward looks at Lucy, but he cannot find out why she is weak.
Dr Seward writes to his old teacher, Professor Van Helsing, in Amsterdam.
Van Helsing comes quickly, looks at Lucy, and looks very serious.
Van Helsing says she needs new blood, and Arthur gives some of his own.
Van Helsing puts garlic flowers in Lucy's room and around her neck.
The next night, Dr Seward gives some of his own blood to Lucy.
On the third night, Van Helsing gives his own blood, and Lucy looks better.
Quincey Morris arrives and gives his blood too, and Lucy sleeps in peace.
Van Helsing goes to Amsterdam and tells Seward to guard Lucy and the garlic.
Lucy's mother does not like the smell, so she takes the garlic away.
Dr Seward is tired, and he goes home to sleep for one night.
Lucy and her mother lie in one bed, and Lucy hears wings at the window.
A big wolf comes to the window, and the glass breaks with a crash.
Lucy's mother sees the wolf and dies from fear in a moment.
Lucy is alone with her dead mother, and the servants will not wake.
In the morning, Dr Seward finds the broken window and a very weak Lucy.
Lucy asks Arthur for a kiss, but Van Helsing pulls him away.
Lucy dies, and in death her face looks sweet and calm.
Lucy is buried in the family tomb at Kingstead on a grey day.
Newspapers say that a beautiful lady takes small children away at night.
Van Helsing tells Seward that some dead people do not rest in their graves.
At night Van Helsing and Seward open Lucy's coffin, and it is empty.
They hide among trees, and a white figure comes with a small child.
Van Helsing lifts a cross, and the white lady cannot come near him.
The next day Arthur is angry when Van Helsing says Lucy is not at rest.
That night they open the coffin, and Lucy lies there, looking alive.
Van Helsing says there is only one way to free her, and Arthur agrees.
Arthur drives a stake into her heart, and Lucy rests in peace at last.
Mr Hawkins dies, and he leaves all his money to Jonathan and Mina.
Jonathan feels stronger now, and he walks with Mina along Piccadilly in London.
Jonathan sees a tall man with a thin face and a pointed beard.
Jonathan turns white and tells Mina that the man is the Count.
That night Mina decides to open the book that Jonathan wrote in the castle.
Mina reads all night, and she believes every terrible word that he wrote.
In the morning Mina tells Jonathan that she believes him, and he is happy.
A telegram says that Professor Van Helsing will come to see Mina.
Mina gives Van Helsing her diary and Jonathan's book, and he reads for hours.
Van Helsing says that Jonathan and Mina must come to Dr Seward's hospital.
Jonathan and Mina go to Dr Seward's hospital, and they meet the group.
Mina listens to Dr Seward's diary on a machine and types it.
Arthur and Quincey arrive, and everyone sits around a big table.
Van Helsing says that the Count is strong, clever, and very old.
The Count fears garlic, holy things, and the light of the sun.
Van Helsing says that they must find all the Count's boxes of earth.
Jonathan says that fifty boxes of earth went from Whitby to Carfax.
From a window, Dr Seward shows them Carfax, next to his hospital.
Mina meets Renfield, who is calm and polite, but sad.
Renfield begs Dr Seward to let him go, but the doctor says no.
At night five men take lamps and walk quietly to the old house.
The old door opens with a loud noise, and a smell of earth comes out.
Inside, the rooms are full of dust, and old webs hang everywhere.
In the old chapel, they count twenty-nine big boxes full of earth.
Suddenly hundreds of rats rush into the room with bright, hungry eyes.
Arthur whistles, and his small dogs come in and chase the rats away.
Van Helsing puts a piece of holy bread in each box.
In the house, Jonathan finds keys and papers for other houses in London.
Next day, Jonathan learns that the other boxes went to three houses.
The men decide to keep Mina away from danger, and she waits sadly.
One evening, Renfield rushes out of the hospital and runs toward Carfax.
Dr Seward follows him and finds him talking to his master at a window.
A huge bat flies over them, and Renfield says that he serves the master.
The men take Renfield back to his room, and he becomes quiet.
Mina feels very tired, and she and Jonathan both sleep too deeply.
Mina has a strange dream of white mist and two red eyes.
Renfield is calm and happy, but he begs Dr Seward to send him away.
In the night, Dr Seward hears a loud cry from Renfield's room.
Renfield whispers that the master is with Mrs Harker, and then he dies.
The men run to Jonathan's room and break down the door.
In the room, a tall pale man holds Mina, and Jonathan lies still.
Van Helsing lifts the holy bread, and the Count turns into mist and escapes.
Mina cries out in pain, and the holy bread burns her forehead.
Jonathan wakes up and cries, and his hair has turned white.
Mina tells her friends what the Count did, and she cries.
Mina asks her friends to promise to free her if she changes.
Van Helsing says that Mina can now feel where the Count is.
The men promise to tell Mina everything, and she joins their group.
The next day, they go to the Count's big house in Piccadilly.
In a dusty room they find boxes of earth, and then a key turns.
The Count walks in, and Jonathan jumps at him with his long knife.
The knife cuts the Count's coat, and gold coins fall on the floor.
The Count jumps through the window and lands in the yard below.
He says that the friends have not won, and his revenge is only starting.
The friends treat the boxes at the other houses in Mile End and Bermondsey.
At dawn, Van Helsing puts Mina into a deep sleep, and she hears water.
Van Helsing says that the Count is on a ship, going far away.
At the docks, they learn that the Czarina Catherine sailed for Varna.
The Count is going home to his castle, and the friends must follow.
The friends take a train to Varna, and Mina goes with them.
The friends take a fast train to Varna, and they wait for the ship.
Every day Mina falls into a trance, but the ship does not come.
A telegram says the ship has gone to Galatz, so they go there.
At Galatz, the captain says that the Count's box was taken away.
Slovak men took the big box up the river on a boat.
The friends split into three groups to follow the box and the Count.
Jonathan and Arthur chase the boat up the river in a small launch.
Quincey and Dr Seward ride horses along the bank of the river.
Van Helsing and Mina go by road toward the mountains and camp at night.
In the dark, three pale women call to Mina, but they cannot come close.
Van Helsing goes to the castle alone and sets three sleeping women free.
He seals the Count's tomb and the door, so the Count cannot return.
The friends close in on the Count's cart as the sun goes down.
Jonathan and Quincey jump on the cart, and their knives end the Count.
Quincey is hurt, and he dies smiling when he sees Mina's clean forehead.
The friends leave the mountains, thankful, and sad for their brave friend.
In England, Jonathan and Mina rebuild their lives, and the past grows quiet.
Seven years later, they have a son, and they name him Quincey.
They visit the old castle again with their son, and it is silent.
Jonathan writes that the papers are only copies, but nobody needs any proof.
B1B2: Jonathan Harker is a young lawyer from London, and he says goodbye to his future wife Mina at the railway station. His employer has sent him far away to meet a rich foreign nobleman called Count Dracula.
The train carries Jonathan through Munich and Vienna, and then he sees Buda-Pesth from the window. He feels that he is leaving the West behind, and everything looks stranger with every mile.

At one station Jonathan eats chicken cooked with red pepper, and he likes it so much that he writes down its name for Mina. He keeps a journal of the whole journey, and he plans to read it to her when he comes home.
In Transylvania Jonathan reads in a guidebook that every old belief in the world seems to live in these mountains. He smiles at the idea, because he is an Englishman and a man of business.

Jonathan reaches the town of Bistritz and goes to the Golden Krone Hotel, where the Count has told him to stay. A letter from Dracula is waiting there, and it says that a coach will take him to the castle.
The landlord and his wife speak very little, and they become pale when Jonathan says the name of the castle. They tell him that they know nothing, but their eyes tell him something quite different.
Just before he leaves, the old woman begs Jonathan not to go, because tomorrow is the eve of St George's Day. She says that at midnight on that night all the evil things in the world are free.

Jonathan is a member of the English Church, and he thinks that a cross is a foolish thing to wear. Still, the woman is kind, so he lets her put it around his neck, and that night he dreams of howling dogs.

The next morning a crowd gathers around the coach, and the people make the sign of the cross and point two fingers at him. He looks up their words in his book and finds that they mean the devil, hell, a witch and a werewolf.
The coach rolls through orchards and green hills, and the driver whips the horses as if he is afraid of being late. Far ahead Jonathan sees the dark mountains, and the sun is already going down.
The coach stops at the top of the Borgo Pass, but there is no carriage there for Jonathan. The other passengers look worried, and the driver says that he must hurry home before dark.

Suddenly four black horses appear out of the dusk, pulling a carriage that makes almost no sound. The driver is very tall, with a long brown beard and a black hat, and his eyes seem to shine red in the lamplight.
The old coachman gives Jonathan's bags to the stranger without a word. Jonathan climbs into the carriage, and the black horses begin to run so fast that the trees seem to rush past him.

The night grows colder, and Jonathan sees the same bend in the road twice, as if the carriage is going round in circles. Far away dogs are howling, and the driver says quietly that the dead travel fast.

Jonathan sees a faint blue flame dancing beside the road, and then another, and the driver stops the horses. He gets down and walks toward the flame, and for a moment Jonathan cannot see what he is doing.
Then the howling comes closer, and grey wolves run out of the trees and circle the carriage. The horses shake with fear, but the driver lifts one arm, and the wolves slowly slip back into the dark.
At last the carriage turns through a huge gate into the yard of a ruined castle with high black walls. The driver lifts down Jonathan's bag as easily as if it were empty and drives away.
Jonathan stands in the silence of the courtyard in front of a great door of carved oak. He wonders if he is dreaming, and he pinches his arm, but the pain is real.
After a long time Jonathan hears slow footsteps and the sound of heavy bolts. The door swings open, and a tall old man in black welcomes Jonathan and asks him to come in freely and of his own will.

When they shake hands, Jonathan feels that the Count's hand is as cold as ice, like the hand of a dead man. The Count carries the bags upstairs himself and leads him to a warm room with a bright fire and a table laid for supper.
Jonathan sleeps late, and the morning sun is already bright when he gets up. He hangs his little shaving mirror on the window and begins to shave in the light.
Suddenly a voice behind him says good morning, and Jonathan jumps and cuts his chin. He looks in the mirror and sees the whole room, but the man standing behind him has no reflection at all.

The Count sees the blood on Jonathan's chin, and his eyes burn as he reaches for his throat. When his hand touches the cross he draws back, tells Jonathan to take care, and throws the mirror out of the window.

Alone again, Jonathan finds a breakfast waiting on a table, but he has not seen a single servant in the castle. He realises that the Count has never eaten or drunk anything while he has been there, and he feels uneasy.

Later Jonathan explores the castle and finds a library full of English books, magazines and newspapers. He is surprised to see how much the Count has read about England, and many of the pages are marked.
The Count comes in at night and asks Jonathan to correct his English. His face is pale and strong, with a high nose, thick eyebrows, sharp white teeth and very red lips.
The Count asks about English law, about lawyers, and about how goods are sent across the sea. Jonathan answers carefully, but he wonders why a nobleman needs to know so much about business.
Jonathan describes the old house at Carfax near London, with its chapel, its pond and its high stone wall. The Count is delighted, and he says that he loves old places because he is old himself.

Late that night the Count speaks proudly of his family, who fought the Turks and led armies for hundreds of years. He says that he is a Szekely, and that the blood of brave soldiers runs in his veins.
Jonathan is listening when a cock crows in the grey light, and the Count suddenly stops speaking. He says that morning is coming, and he leaves the room in a hurry.

One evening the Count asks Jonathan to stay for a whole month and to write to Mr Hawkins about it. Jonathan does not dare to refuse a rich client, so he writes the letter, although he does not feel easy.
Before the Count leaves, he warns Jonathan not to sleep in any other room of the castle. He says that the old rooms are not safe, and that any man who sleeps in them will have terrible dreams.

A few days later Jonathan says that he is ready to go home, and that Mr Hawkins will be waiting for news. The Count opens the great door, but wolves are howling in the dark, and he closes it again with a cold smile.

That night Jonathan tries every door in the castle, and every one of them is locked. He understands at last that he is not a guest but a prisoner, and he writes in shorthand so that nobody can read it.

The Count tells Jonathan to write three more letters, and to put dates on them that are weeks away. The first says his work is nearly done, the next that he is starting home, and the last that he has reached Bistritz.
One night Jonathan looks out of his window and sees the Count come out of a window below. He crawls head first down the wall like a lizard, with his black cloak spreading out like wings.

Jonathan decides to explore, and he finds an unlocked door at the end of a long passage. It opens into a quiet room with old furniture and a window full of moonlight, and there he sits down and falls asleep.

Jonathan wakes to find three young women in the room with him, one fair and two dark. They move without a sound, they have long white teeth and red lips, and they whisper about who will kiss him first.
The fair woman bends over Jonathan's throat, and he closes his eyes and waits. Suddenly the Count rushes in, pulls her away, and says angrily that this man belongs to him.

The Count promises the women that they may kiss Jonathan when he has finished with him, and he gives them a bag. Something inside the bag cries like a child, and Jonathan faints and wakes up in his own bed.
Jonathan wakes in his own bed, and his clothes are folded on a chair in a way that is not his. His watch has not been wound, and he knows that someone must have carried him there.
A few days later Jonathan sees the Count walk out of the castle wearing Jonathan's own travelling suit. He understands that the villagers will see the Count and think that it is Jonathan.
A woman runs to the castle gate and screams to the Count to give her back her child. The wolves rush out of the forest, and soon her cries are heard no more.

Jonathan goes into the Count's room, which is empty, and finds a great heap of gold coins from Rome, Hungary, Greece and Turkey. Many of them are so old that their dates cannot be read, and in the corner there is a heavy door.
Behind the door a spiral stair leads down into a passage under the castle. The air smells of old earth, and Jonathan follows the passage into the dark with a shaking hand.

At the end of the passage lies an old chapel with broken tombs, and its floor is covered with big wooden boxes. Each box is full of fresh earth, and Jonathan sees that they have been moved here very recently.

In the biggest box Jonathan finds the Count lying on a heap of earth, and he looks like a dead man. His eyes are open but he does not breathe, and his face is fuller and his lips are redder than before.

Jonathan lifts a spade and strikes at the face, but the head turns and the eyes glare at him with terrible hatred. The spade glances off and makes only a small cut, and Jonathan runs back up the stair, shaking from head to foot.

Soon afterwards strong men arrive with rough carts, and Jonathan watches from his window as they nail down the lids of the boxes. The carts rattle out through the gate, and he is left alone in the silent castle with the three women.

Jonathan knows that the Count will soon leave for England, and he does not want to wait for the women. He writes a last goodbye to Mina and climbs out of the window, because he would rather risk the wall than die as a prisoner.
Mina Murray is a teacher at a school in Exeter, and she writes often to her friend Lucy. She is learning shorthand and typing, because she wants to help Jonathan with his work after they are married.

Lucy Westenra is a lively and pretty girl, and she writes to Mina in great excitement. She says that three men have asked her to marry them in a single day, and that she must tell the whole story at once.
The first man is Dr John Seward, a young doctor with a strong, serious face. Lucy likes him very much, but she does not love him, so she says no as kindly as she can.
The second man is Quincey Morris, a tall and cheerful American from Texas. He asks in a funny, friendly way, and when Lucy says no, he shakes her hand and says that he will always be her friend.

The third man is Arthur Holmwood, the son of a lord, and he is the one whom Lucy loves. When he asks her, she bursts into tears and says yes, although she wishes that she could make all three men happy.
Dr Seward is the head of a hospital for troubled minds near London, and he keeps his diary on a phonograph. After Lucy's refusal he feels very sad, so he tries to forget his sorrow by working harder.
One of Dr Seward's patients is a man named Renfield, who is strong, clever and about fifty years old. He is very polite, but he has a strange habit that the doctor wants to understand.
Renfield catches flies in his room and keeps them in a box, and he eats them. He uses the flies to feed spiders, and the spiders to feed birds, and he says that he is collecting life.
That evening Quincey asks his two friends, Seward and Arthur, to come and drink to Lucy's health. They feel sad and glad at the same time, and they promise that they will be friends whatever happens.
Mina has had only a few short letters from Jonathan, and now none comes at all. She is worried, so she accepts Lucy's invitation to stay at the seaside town of Whitby.
Mina arrives at Whitby on a warm July day, and Lucy and her mother meet her at the station. Lucy looks happy and healthy, and the two friends talk without stopping all the way to the house.
Whitby is a beautiful old town, with red roofs that climb the hillside above a busy harbour. On the high cliff stand the ruins of an old abbey, and a long flight of steps leads up to the church.
In the afternoon Mina and Lucy climb up to the churchyard, which stands high above the sea. There are seats beside the graves, and they like to sit there and watch the ships come and go.
On one of the seats they often meet an old sailor named Mr Swales, who talks to everyone. He says that many of the stones are for men lost at sea, whose bodies are not buried there at all.
Mr Swales says that he is more than ninety years old, and that the sea has taken many of his friends. He laughs when he speaks about death, and he says that he will go when the time comes.
In the evening Mina writes in her journal by the window of her room. She has had no letter from Jonathan for weeks, and she cannot stop thinking about him.

Mrs Westenra tells Mina that Lucy walked in her sleep when she was younger, and that it sometimes comes back when she is upset. Mina promises to lock the door at night and tie the key to her wrist, so that Lucy cannot go out alone.
A letter from Arthur arrives for Lucy at breakfast, and she reads it three times and smiles. His father is ill, and he must stay in London, but he promises that he will soon come to Whitby.
The next day is hot and very still, and there is not a breath of wind on the sea. The old sailors look at the sky and the water, and they say that something is wrong with the weather.
At sunset the sky turns a deep red, and the fishing boats hurry back into the harbour. The coastguard tells the people on the cliff that a great storm is coming.
That night a terrible storm comes in from the sea, and the waves smash against the harbour wall. Half the town stands on the cliff in the wind and watches, and Mina holds Lucy's arm.

Through the rain and the flashing lightning, a schooner with all its sails set races toward the harbour. The coastguard turns his great light on it, and everyone sees that a man stands at the wheel but does not move.
The ship rushes past the end of the pier and drives itself onto the sand under the East Cliff. The crash is so loud that Mina feels it in the rock beneath her feet.
At the moment the ship touches the shore, a huge dog leaps from the deck onto the sand. It runs up the cliff toward the churchyard, and it vanishes into the darkness.
A coastguard climbs onto the ship and goes to the wheel. The captain is dead, and his hands are tied to the wheel with cords, and a cross is wound around his fingers.
In the dead man's pocket the men find a log in a bottle, and it tells where the ship has been. The Demeter left Varna with fifty big boxes of earth, and the boxes were meant for a lawyer in Whitby.
The log says that the crew grew afraid, because men began to disappear in the night. One by one they vanished, and the mate swore that he had seen a tall, thin stranger walking on the deck.
At last the mate went mad with fear and jumped into the sea, and only the captain was left. He wrote that he would tie himself to the wheel with a cross, so that nothing could take him from his post.
Three days later the whole town walks in a long line behind the captain's coffin. The boats in the harbour fly their flags, and many people cry, even though they never knew the man.
The next morning someone finds old Mr Swales dead on his seat in the churchyard. His neck is broken, and his face looks as if he saw something terrible in the night.
In the middle of the night Mina wakes and sees that Lucy's bed is empty. She throws on a shawl and runs out into the dark streets with her heart beating fast.
The moon is bright over the cliff, and Mina can see the seat in the churchyard from far away. Lucy is sitting there, white in the moonlight, and a long dark shape is bending over her.
When Mina arrives, the dark shape has gone, and Lucy lies back with her head thrown over the seat. There are two small red marks on her throat, and Mina fastens her shawl with a pin to keep her warm.
Mina brings Lucy home without waking her, and the next morning Lucy remembers nothing. She says only that she had a strange dream, and that her neck feels a little sore.
A few days later a letter arrives from Sister Agatha, a nurse in a hospital in Budapest. She writes that Jonathan Harker is there, and that he has been very ill with a brain fever.
Sister Agatha says that Jonathan talks about wolves and blood and strange horrors, and that he calls for Mina. Mina leaves Lucy with her mother and takes the first train to Budapest.
At the hospital Mina finds Jonathan thin, pale and much older than before, but he knows her at once. He holds out his arms to her, and they cry together.
Jonathan gives Mina his shorthand journal and asks her not to read it unless a solemn duty makes it necessary. Mina ties it with a ribbon and seals it with wax, and she promises to keep it safe.
Jonathan and Mina are married in the hospital chapel, with Sister Agatha as a witness. Mina is happy even though her husband is still weak, and she is proud to be his wife.
They return to England, and Mr Hawkins welcomes them kindly in Exeter. Slowly Jonathan grows stronger, but he often wakes in the night, and Mina holds his hand until he sleeps again.
Lucy goes back to London with her mother, but she sleeps badly and grows pale. At night she hears a large bat flapping at her window, and she feels very tired in the morning.
Arthur is worried about Lucy, but he must stay with his father, who is seriously ill. He asks his good friend Dr Seward to look at her and to tell him the truth.
Dr Seward finds Lucy as cheerful as ever, but she is pale and thin. He cannot find any disease in her, and her blood seems to be getting weaker every day.

Dr Seward does not understand the case, so he writes to his old teacher, Professor Van Helsing, in Amsterdam. Van Helsing is a famous doctor who knows many strange things, and he comes by the next boat.
Van Helsing is a short, strong man with a broad face and kind, clever eyes. He looks at Lucy for a long time, and when he sees the marks on her throat he becomes very serious.
Van Helsing says that Lucy needs fresh blood at once, and Arthur is the first to give it. His blood flows into her arm, and soon the colour comes back to her cheeks.

Van Helsing brings a big bunch of garlic flowers and puts them around Lucy's room and around her neck. Lucy laughs at the smell, but he tells her that it is medicine and that she must never take it away.
The next night Dr Seward gives some of his own blood to Lucy while Van Helsing watches. When Lucy wakes in the morning she is a little stronger, but the doctors are still worried.
On the third night Van Helsing gives his own blood to Lucy, although he is tired. By morning she smiles, and for the first time in many days she eats a good breakfast.
On the next night Quincey Morris arrives and gives his blood too, saying that he is glad to help. Lucy sleeps in peace, and the three men sit by her bed and hope.
Van Helsing must go home to Amsterdam for a few days, and he tells Seward to guard Lucy day and night. He says that the windows must stay closed and the garlic must stay in the room.
Lucy's mother does not like the smell of garlic, and she thinks that Lucy needs fresh air. She takes the flowers away and opens the window, and Lucy is too tired to stop her.
Dr Seward is very tired after many sleepless nights, and he goes home to rest for one night. He leaves Lucy with her mother, and Van Helsing's telegram, which tells him not to go, comes too late.
That night Lucy and her mother lie in the same bed, and the house is very quiet. Lucy hears the flapping of wings at the window, and somewhere in the dark she hears the howl of a wolf.
Suddenly the head of a huge grey wolf appears at the window, and the glass breaks with a crash. The animal has escaped from the zoo, and its eyes shine in the dark like two burning coals.
Lucy's mother sees the wolf, and the shock is too great for her weak heart. She falls back across the bed and dies, and the garlic wreath is torn from Lucy's neck.
Lucy cannot move, because her dead mother lies across her, and she is too weak to push her away. She calls for the servants, but they are in a deep sleep and nobody comes.

In the morning Dr Seward arrives and finds the broken window, the servants asleep, and Lucy lying very still. He sends for Van Helsing, who hurries from the station and puts new garlic around the room.
Arthur comes, and Lucy looks at him with strange, bright eyes and asks him for a kiss. Van Helsing pulls him back, because he sees something in her face that makes him afraid.
That night Lucy dies, and for a moment her face looks sweet, calm and beautiful again. Arthur kisses her gently, and Van Helsing watches them sadly, for he knows what may follow.
On a grey day Lucy is buried in her family's tomb at Kingstead, next to her mother. Arthur is crying, and Van Helsing stands a little apart and watches the tomb with kind, worried eyes.

A few days later the newspapers tell a strange story about children who have been lost in the park at night. They say that a beautiful lady has taken them away, and each child has two small marks on the throat.

Van Helsing takes Seward to see one of the children, and Seward is shocked that the small wounds look like Lucy's. Then the professor says quietly that some dead people do not rest in their graves, and that they must be stopped.
At night the two men go to Lucy's tomb and open the coffin, and Seward finds that it is empty. He is shaking with fear, but Van Helsing tells him calmly to hide and to wait.
They hide among the yew trees in the dark churchyard until a white figure comes slowly toward the tomb. It is carrying a small child in its arms, and Seward recognises the way it walks.
Van Helsing opens his lantern, and the light shows Lucy's face, which is no longer sweet but cruel and hungry. She drops the child, and when he holds up a cross she cannot come near him.
The next day Van Helsing tells Arthur and Quincey the truth, and Arthur is so angry that he almost hits him. Then he sees how serious the professor is, and he agrees to come to the tomb that night.
That night the four men open the coffin again, and Lucy lies there, more beautiful than she was in life. Her lips are red and her cheeks are rosy, and Arthur stares at her in horror.
Van Helsing explains that the only way to free Lucy's soul is to drive a wooden stake through her heart. Arthur is pale, but he says that he wants to do it himself, because he loves her.
Arthur takes the hammer and the stake, and he drives it into her heart while Van Helsing reads the prayers. Lucy's face grows calm and sweet, and at last she rests in peace.
Old Mr Hawkins dies suddenly, and he leaves all his money and his house to Jonathan and Mina. They are very sad, because he was like a father to them.
After the funeral Jonathan and Mina go to live in London, and Jonathan grows stronger every week. On a bright afternoon they walk along Piccadilly together, arm in arm, and look at the shops.
Suddenly Jonathan stops, and his face turns as white as paper. Across the street a tall man with a thin face, a black moustache and a pointed beard is staring at a pretty girl.
Jonathan whispers that it is the Count, and that he has grown young. The man sees them, and his eyes burn with anger for a moment before he steps into a cab and drives away.
Mina takes Jonathan to a tea shop, where he sits trembling and cannot speak. That night she decides that the solemn duty has come, and she breaks the wax seal on his journal.
Mina reads all night by the lamp, and she is more frightened with every page. At last she understands that the terrible story is true, and that a monster is walking in London.
In the morning Mina tells Jonathan that she has read his journal and believes every word. He cries with relief, because he has been afraid that he was going mad.
Mina has written to Dr Seward to ask about Lucy, and he answers that Professor Van Helsing wishes to meet her. The professor sends a telegram saying that he will come the next morning.
The next morning Van Helsing arrives, and Mina gives him her own diary and Jonathan's journal. He reads for hours, and she sees his face grow bright with hope.
When he has finished, he thanks Mina and says that her husband is a brave man. He invites them both to Dr Seward's hospital, where a small band of friends will fight the Count.

Jonathan and Mina arrive at Dr Seward's hospital at Purfleet and meet the doctor, who is kind and tired. Next to the hospital Jonathan sees a high stone wall, and behind it stands the old house of Carfax.
Dr Seward keeps his diary on a phonograph, and Mina offers to type it for the others. As she listens to his sad voice she learns what happened to Lucy, and she cries for her friend.
Arthur and Quincey arrive, and the whole group sits around a table with Mina's typed pages in front of them. They have all read the story, and not one of them laughs.

Van Helsing stands up and tells them that Count Dracula is a vampire who has lived for hundreds of years. He is as strong as twenty men, and he can control wolves, rats and bats and turn himself into a wolf or a bat.
But the Count has weaknesses too, says Van Helsing, and he fears garlic and holy things. He cannot enter a house unless someone invites him, and the light of the sun takes away most of his power.
Van Helsing says that the Count must rest in earth from his own country, so the friends must find every box. If they make every box unfit for him with holy bread, he will have nowhere to sleep.
Jonathan explains how he helped the Count to buy Carfax, and he says that the fifty boxes came by ship to Whitby. From there they went by train to London, and then they were carried to the old house.
