Dr Seward takes them to a window and shows them the old house of Carfax behind its high wall. Its windows are dark and dusty, and it stands only a few minutes' walk from his patients.
Mina visits Renfield, who is calm and polite and bows to her when she comes into the room. She notices that he looks sad, and she wonders how a gentle man can have such a strange illness.
Renfield begs Dr Seward to let him go, and he says that he will be good if he is free. Seward cannot trust him, so he refuses, and Renfield sits down on his bed with a bitter look.
At night the five men take lamps, keys and holy things and walk across the dark ground to Carfax. Mina stays at the hospital, and she watches them go until she can no longer see their lights.
Jonathan opens the old front door with a key, and it swings open with a loud groan. A bad smell of old earth comes out, and the men cover their faces with their hands.
Inside, the rooms are full of dust, and thick spider webs hang from the ceilings. The lamps make long shadows on the walls, and the men move quietly from room to room.
In the old chapel they find big wooden boxes full of fresh earth, and they begin to count them. There are twenty-nine boxes, and the Count brought fifty, so twenty-one are somewhere else.
Suddenly the floor seems to move, and hundreds of rats rush into the chapel with bright, hungry eyes. They are much larger than ordinary rats, and the men step back in fear.
Arthur puts two fingers in his mouth and whistles, and his small terrier dogs run in. The rats scream and run away in every direction, and soon the chapel is quiet again.
Van Helsing takes a piece of holy bread from a small box and puts it into each box of earth. He says that now the Count can no longer use them, because the earth is no longer clean for him.

In the study Jonathan finds bundles of keys with labels, and papers for houses in Piccadilly, Mile End and Bermondsey. The Count has bought other houses in London, and the friends must search all of them.
The next morning Jonathan goes to the carriers' office and learns where the missing boxes went. They were taken to three houses, one in Piccadilly, one in Mile End and one in Bermondsey.
Back at the hospital the men decide that Mina must not be taken into danger again. She agrees sadly, and she stays at home with her typewriter and her worries.
One evening Renfield rushes out of the hospital through a door that someone left open. He runs across the grass toward Carfax, and Dr Seward and two nurses run after him.

Dr Seward finds Renfield at the old house, standing under a window and talking to somebody that nobody can see. He is calling the person his master, and he says that he is ready to do whatever the master wants.
A huge bat flies silently over their heads and disappears into the dark. Renfield cries out that he serves the master, and the nurses have to hold him tightly.
The nurses take Renfield back to his room, and soon he is quiet and sad. He will not say why he ran, and Dr Seward writes in his diary that he does not understand the man.
At the same time Mina feels very tired in the mornings, and she and Jonathan both sleep much too deeply. She tells herself that it is only worry, but she cannot shake off the strange weakness.
One night Mina dreams of a white mist that creeps under the door and fills the room. In the middle of the mist she sees two red eyes, and she cannot move or call out.
In the daytime Renfield is calm and cheerful, and Dr Seward is surprised by the change. Then the patient begs him to send him to another place far from Purfleet, and Seward says no.
In the middle of that night Dr Seward is woken by a cry from Renfield's room. He runs there with a lamp and finds the man lying on the floor, badly hurt.
Renfield opens his eyes and whispers that the master came to his window and then went to Mrs Harker's room. He says that he tried to stop him, and then he dies.
Seward, Van Helsing, Arthur and Quincey run along the corridor to the room where Jonathan and Mina are sleeping. The door is locked, and Quincey throws himself against it until it breaks.

The door bursts open, and the friends see a terrible sight in the moonlight of the bedroom. Jonathan lies on the bed like a dead man, and a tall, thin man in black holds Mina and presses her face against his chest.
The Count turns on them with burning red eyes, and Van Helsing holds up the holy bread to stop him. The Count draws back, turns into a white mist, and slips away under the door.
Mina rises from the floor, and she cries that she is unclean and must not touch her husband. Van Helsing touches her forehead with the holy bread, and it leaves a red mark like a burn.
Jonathan wakes up, and when he sees Mina's pale face and the blood, he cries aloud. By the morning his hair has turned white, and Mina holds his hand and tells him that she loves him.
Mina tells the friends everything, though it is very hard for her, and she says that the Count came in a mist. He made her drink his blood, and he promised to make her one of his own.
Mina asks her friends to make a solemn promise: if she ever changes into a vampire, they must free her. Van Helsing agrees at once, and one by one the others promise too, with tears in their eyes.
Van Helsing explains that because of the Count's mark, Mina can sometimes feel where he is. He says that this is a danger, but that it can also be used as a weapon against him.
The men promise that there will be no more secrets, and that Mina will be part of the group from now on. She thanks them quietly, and she says that she will help them in every way she can.
The next morning the friends travel to Piccadilly and go to the big empty house that the Count has bought. Jonathan opens the front door with the key, and a smell of old earth meets them in the hall.
In a dusty room at the back of the house the friends find the Count's boxes of earth. As Van Helsing begins to treat them with holy bread, they hear a key turn in the front door.
The door opens, and Count Dracula walks into the hall with a calm face and cold eyes. Jonathan springs at him with his long, curved knife, but the Count leaps aside.
The knife cuts through the Count's coat, and a rain of gold coins and papers falls on the floor. The Count's face is white with anger, and for a moment he looks like a wild animal.
Then the Count dives through the window, and the glass breaks around him as he falls to the yard below. He stands up among the broken pieces and looks back at the friends with a cruel smile.

He tells them that they cannot stop him, because he has other places to rest and his revenge has only begun. He says that the people they love are already his, and then he vanishes into the stable behind the house.
The friends gather the gold and the papers, and then they go to Mile End and Bermondsey. In each house they find boxes of earth, and they put holy bread in all of them.
At sunrise Van Helsing puts Mina into a deep sleep and asks her what she can feel. She says that she hears water lapping, wood creaking and the wind in ropes, and that everything around her is dark.

Van Helsing understands that the Count is lying in his box on a ship, and that he is leaving England. He says that they are lucky, because the Count must stay in his box all day and cannot escape from the ship.
The friends go to the docks and learn that only one ship has left that night for Varna. It is called the Czarina Catherine, and a large strange box was put on board at the last moment.
Van Helsing says that the Count is going home to his castle, where he is safe and strong. The friends decide to follow him, to reach his country before he does, and to destroy him there.
Mina says that she will not stay behind, because she is the only one who can feel the Count. The others agree, and the whole group takes a train across Europe toward the Black Sea.

The friends travel by train across Europe to Varna and take rooms at a hotel by the sea. They ask about the Czarina Catherine, but the ship has not arrived, and every day they wait with growing worry.

Each morning and evening Van Helsing puts Mina into a trance, and she tells him what she can feel. She says that she hears the same sounds of water and wood, and that the ship is moving, but the harbour stays empty.
At last a telegram comes to say that the ship has been sent to another port, Galatz, on the river. The friends hurry back to the station, and they take the next train to Galatz.

At Galatz the friends find the Czarina Catherine in the harbour, and the captain tells them what happened. He says that a thick fog followed the ship all the way, and that a man took a large box away at once.
The man who took the box was an agent of the Count, and he gave it to Slovak men with a cart. The Slovaks put it on a boat, and the boat went up the river Sereth that same night.

Van Helsing decides that the friends must split into three groups, because the Count could leave the river at any place. He will take Mina by road to the castle, and the others will follow the boat by water and by land.
Jonathan and Arthur buy a fast steam launch and chase the boat up the river. They ask at every village, and they push the little engine as hard as it will go.
Quincey and Dr Seward buy strong horses and ride along the river bank, in case the boat turns toward the land. They carry rifles and keep watch on the water, and Quincey enjoys the chase.

Van Helsing and Mina travel by carriage on rough mountain roads toward the Borgo Pass. On the way Mina falls into trances, and she says that she can hear cattle, creaking wheels and the sound of men's voices.

At night Van Helsing makes a big circle of holy bread crumbs around the fire and sits with Mina inside it. Three pale women come out of the mist, and they call softly to her, but they cannot cross the circle.
At dawn Van Helsing leaves Mina inside the circle and tells her not to move. He climbs to the castle alone, finds three tombs in the old chapel, and sets the women free.
Then Van Helsing finds the Count's own tomb and puts holy bread inside it. He closes the great door of the castle, so that the Count can never rest there again.

That afternoon the friends close in from three sides on the mountain road, and Mina says that the Count is very near. Soon they see a cart with a big box racing toward the castle, with armed men all around it.

Jonathan and Quincey leap onto the cart and fight their way to the box as the sun touches the mountains. Jonathan's long knife cuts the Count's throat, Quincey's knife strikes his heart, and the Count crumbles into dust.
Quincey is badly hurt in the fight, and he lies on the ground with his friends around him. He smiles when he sees that the mark on Mina's forehead has gone, and he dies happy.
The friends turn away from the mountains in sorrow, because they have lost a brave friend. They are thankful that the evil is gone, and Mina's face is peaceful at last.
In England, Jonathan and Mina rebuild their lives, and Arthur and Seward both marry happily. The memory of the adventure grows quiet, but they never forget the friends who stood beside them.

Seven years later Jonathan and Mina have a little son, whose birthday is the same day as Quincey's death. They name him Quincey, and Mina believes that some of the brave American's spirit lives in him.
That summer the family visits the mountains of Transylvania, and they walk over the old ground. The castle still stands high above the quiet valley, but every trace of the horror has gone.
Back at home, Jonathan sees that the old papers are only typed copies, so there is no real proof. Van Helsing holds the boy on his knee and says that one day he will learn how brave his mother is.
C1C2: On a grey morning Jonathan Harker, a young solicitor with a good heart and a careful mind, says goodbye to his fiancée Mina Murray on a London platform. His employer, Mr Hawkins, has sent him on a long errand to a foreign nobleman who wishes to buy a house in England. He steps onto the train with a light heart, never suspecting that the journey will change his life for ever.

The train carries him across Europe through Munich and Vienna, and from the carriage window he glimpses Buda-Pesth, bright with domes and bridges and already strange to an English eye. At every stop the clothes, the faces and the languages grow less familiar, and Jonathan has the curious sense of leaving the modern world behind him. He notes in his journal that the trains are late, as though the East kept time by some other clock.

At a station dinner Jonathan is served a dish of chicken cooked with red pepper, a recipe so good that he writes its name in his notebook for Mina. He is a faithful keeper of journals and records everything, from the cost of the meal to the colour of the sky. It is a habit that will one day matter far more than he can now imagine.

As the train climbs into Transylvania, Jonathan studies a guidebook and learns that this land lies inside a great horseshoe of mountains where every kind of superstition seems to gather. The authors mention ghosts, charms and fears that have survived there for centuries, and he reads these passages with the amused superior air of a man brought up among railways and law books. Nothing in all his experience of courts and contracts has prepared him for what lies ahead.

At last he reaches the old town of Bistritz and goes to the Golden Krone Hotel, which the Count has chosen for his first night. A letter from Dracula is waiting at the desk, written in careful English and promising that a coach will take him through the mountains to the castle. It welcomes him warmly, and yet something in its polite phrases leaves him with a faint chill.

The landlord and his wife, who have been so cheerful until now, fall silent when Jonathan names the place he is going to. They exchange a long look, mutter that they know nothing, and refuse to say another word, even though he tries again in the best German he can find. Jonathan decides to stay calm, but their frightened faces stay with him for the rest of the evening.

On the eve of his departure the landlord's wife seizes his hand and pleads with him to put off the journey, because the coming night is the eve of St George's Day. She tells him that at midnight on that night all the evil things in the world are said to have full power, and she asks if he truly understands where he is going. Jonathan thanks her politely and promises to be careful, though in truth he does not believe a word of it.

When her pleading fails, the old woman takes a small cross from her own neck and presses it into Jonathan's hand. A man of the Church of England, he thinks such trinkets foolish, but he cannot refuse a gift offered with so much feeling, and he hangs it around his neck. That night he sleeps badly and dreams of dogs howling beneath his window, a long way off.

In the morning a crowd has gathered around the waiting coach, and as Jonathan climbs in the people cross themselves and point two fingers at him. He catches a few strange words, and when he looks them up in his guidebook he is dismayed to find that they mean Satan, hell, witch and something between a werewolf and a vampire. He tells himself, rather uneasily, that this is only the way of simple people.

The coach rattles out of the town and into a gentle country of orchards, meadows and wooded slopes, where the afternoon sun lies warm on the grass. Yet the driver whips his horses as though pursued, and Jonathan sees the high mountains growing larger and darker ahead, their peaks dusted with snow. The light is already beginning to fade as the road turns toward the Borgo Pass.

The coach halts at the top of the Borgo Pass, but no carriage waits there to carry Jonathan on to the castle, and the cold wind seems to sharpen as the light fades. The other travellers grow restless, whispering to one another and glancing at the dark forest, while the driver mutters that he must be gone before nightfall. Jonathan, left alone with his luggage on the empty road, begins to wonder whether his host has forgotten him.

Then four black horses come out of the dusk, drawing a light carriage that seems to make no sound on the stony road, and the driver who sits above them is the tallest man Jonathan has ever seen. He has a long brown beard, a black hat pulled low over his face, and eyes that seem to glow red when the lamplight touches them. The old coachman hurries to hand over the baggage, and the passengers cross themselves as the stranger takes it.

Jonathan is helped into the strange carriage, and with a crack of the whip the black horses leap forward and carry him into the darkness at a terrifying pace. The pines on either side blur into a single wall, and the wind howls past his ears like a living thing. He clings to the seat and tells himself that the driver, whoever he is, must be taking him where the Count intends.

The hours pass, and it seems to Jonathan that the carriage is passing the same bend in the road for a second time, as though it travels in a great circle through the dark. Somewhere far off dogs begin to howl, one after another, until the whole night is full of their cries. The driver, who has not spoken once, murmurs in German that the dead travel fast, and Jonathan decides that he must have misheard him.

Beside the road Jonathan notices a small blue flame, faint and quivering, and then a second one a little further on, and the driver pulls up the horses suddenly. He gets down and walks to the nearest flame, and by some trick of the light Jonathan cannot see clearly what he is doing there. When he returns, the carriage races on again, and Jonathan wonders whether the whole strange scene was a dream.

All at once the howling draws near, and a ring of grey wolves with shining eyes and lolling red tongues closes in around the carriage. The horses scream and shake with terror, and Jonathan is too frightened even to cry out. Then the driver stands up, raises one arm in a slow, commanding gesture, and the wolves draw back and melt away into the shadows as if they had been told to go.

After hours that seem endless, the carriage rattles through a vast gateway and into the courtyard of a castle so large and ruinous that Jonathan can see little but black walls against the moon. Not one of its many windows is lit, and the silence that hangs over the whole place feels strangely unnatural. The driver lifts Jonathan's heavy bag down as lightly as a bundle of straw, and before he can say a word of thanks the carriage is gone.

Jonathan is left alone in the great court before a massive door carved with old patterns, and the silence is so deep that he can hear his own heart. He wonders whether he has fallen asleep on the coach and is dreaming it all, and he pinches his arm hard to make sure he is awake. The sting is real, and he stands still, listening for any sound from inside the castle.

At last he hears slow steps and the grinding of great bolts, and the door opens to show a tall old man in black from head to foot, holding a silver lamp. The man speaks in perfect English, though with a strange, careful music, and bids him welcome to his house and to enter freely and of his own will. Jonathan steps across the threshold, and the Count takes his hand in a grip so cold that it might have been carved from ice.

The Count refuses all help with the luggage, picks up the heavy bags himself, and leads Jonathan up winding stairs and along stone passages to a room where a bright fire is burning. A table has been laid there with a hot supper, and a bedroom lies beyond it, but not a single servant is to be seen anywhere. Jonathan is tired and grateful, yet he cannot help noticing how oddly quiet the great house is.

Jonathan sleeps far later than he intends, and when he wakes the sun is high above the mountains and a plain breakfast is waiting on the table. He hangs his small shaving mirror from the window frame, lathers his face and settles down to put himself in order before meeting his host. He is humming quietly, and he feels almost cheerful for the first time since he left Bistritz.

Without any warning a voice behind him says good morning, and Jonathan, startled, cuts himself with the razor. He turns to look in the glass and sees the whole room clearly, with its bed and its window and its door, but the tall man standing at his shoulder has no reflection at all. A cold shiver runs through him, because a mirror shows the truth about a room and does not lie.

The Count sees the bright drop of blood on Jonathan's chin, and his eyes blaze with a sudden fury as his hand reaches toward his guest's throat. Then his fingers brush the little cross that hangs there, and he draws back at once, as if the metal had burned him. He warns Jonathan to take more care in this country, snatches the mirror from its place, and hurls it out of the window into the courtyard below.

Alone again, Jonathan goes into the next room and finds a breakfast set out for him, though he has not seen a servant since his arrival. He realises, with growing alarm, that in all the hours he has spent with the Count his host has not once eaten or drunk anything. The thought troubles him far more than the broken mirror, and he cannot make it go away.

During the long daylight hours, when the Count is nowhere to be found, Jonathan wanders through the castle and discovers a library filled with English books, magazines and newspapers. There are volumes on law, on history, on travel and on the customs of London, many of them marked and worn with use. It is clear that the Count has studied England with the patience of a man preparing a long and careful campaign.

When evening falls the Count returns and sits by the fire, and Jonathan can study his face at leisure: a strong, pale face with a high thin nose, heavy eyebrows, red lips and teeth that are unusually sharp. He asks Jonathan to correct his English, for although he speaks it well he fears that he will sound strange in London. His breath smells faintly foul, and Jonathan sees that the palms of his hands are covered with hair.

The Count questions him long into the night about English law, the work of a solicitor, and the best way to send goods and money across the sea. Jonathan answers as carefully as he can, though it puzzles him that a nobleman should want to know so much about the dull details of business. The Count nods and listens like a student who intends to remember every word.

Then Jonathan shows him the papers for the house at Carfax, an old estate near the village of Purfleet, with a chapel, a pond and a high wall of stone. The Count is delighted that it is ancient and full of shadows, saying that he is old himself and has no taste for sunshine or merry company. He does not seem to mind when Jonathan adds that a private hospital stands close by.

As the fire burns low, the Count speaks with pride of his family and tells how his people, the Szekelys, held the border against the Turks and claimed the blood of Attila himself. He talks of the old wars as if he had seen them with his own eyes, saying we and us, and his voice rises like a trumpet. Jonathan listens spellbound and tries not to wonder how a man can remember so well what happened so long ago.

At the first crow of a cock in the grey dawn, the Count stops in the middle of a sentence and stands up as if some invisible hand had pulled him. He bids Jonathan a hasty and courteous goodnight and sweeps out of the room, leaving the fire dying and the window turning pale. Jonathan stays awake for some time, listening to the silence of the sleeping castle.

One evening, as they sit by the fire, the Count asks Jonathan to stay in the castle for a whole month and to write at once to Mr Hawkins to explain. Jonathan would much rather go home, but he cannot refuse so important a client, and he sees that the request is not really a request at all. He writes the letter in his neatest hand, and the Count takes it away with a courteous smile.

Before he leaves for the night, the Count gives Jonathan a serious warning never to sleep in any other room of the castle than his own. The old chambers, he says, are not safe, and any man who sleeps in them will have dreams that no sane person wants to have. Jonathan promises to obey, and he tells himself that his host is only thinking of his comfort.

A few days later Jonathan says that he must go home soon because Mr Hawkins will be waiting for news, and the Count answers that he is perfectly free to leave. He walks to the great door, draws back the heavy bolts and opens it, and at once the howling of wolves rolls in from the black night. Jonathan understands the lesson at last, and the Count, with a smile as cold as the stone around them, closes the door and slides the bolts home again.

Left to himself, Jonathan tries every door in the castle one after another, and he finds that each of them is locked or barred. The great gate to the courtyard is shut fast, and the windows that look out over the precipice are far too high to climb through. At last the truth is plain to him, that he is no honoured guest but a prisoner, and he begins to write his journal in shorthand so that no one else can read it.

The Count now asks him to write three letters and to date them several weeks ahead, saying that his work is nearly done, that he is starting for home, and that he has reached Bistritz. Jonathan sees at once the cold purpose behind this request, for if the letters are believed, nobody in England will begin to look for him. He signs them with a trembling hand, because he knows that a refusal would be dangerous.

That night, looking out of his window, Jonathan sees the Count climb through a window further down and begin to crawl head first down the sheer wall of the castle. His black cloak spreads out around him like great wings, and his fingers and toes find holds in the cracked stones as easily as those of a lizard. Jonathan watches in horror until the figure vanishes into the shadows far below, and he wonders what kind of man, or creature, he has been living with.

Desperate to learn anything that might help him escape, Jonathan breaks the Count's warning and explores a wing of the castle where he has not been before. At the end of a long passage he finds a door that opens, and behind it lies a quiet room with old furniture and a window flooded with moonlight. He sits down on a couch to write a letter to Mina, and before he knows it he has fallen asleep.

He wakes with a start and sees three young women standing in the moonlight, two dark and one fair, who have come into the room without a single sound. Their teeth are very white and their lips very red, and they whisper and laugh as they argue over which of them shall kiss him first. Jonathan is afraid to move, for there is something in their beauty that he feels as both a longing and a terror.

The fair one kneels over him and bends her head to his throat, and he closes his eyes and waits for what must come. At that moment the Count rushes into the room like a storm, seizes her and flings her aside, and his face is white with fury. He tells the women, in a low and terrible voice, that Jonathan belongs to him and that none of them may touch him.

The Count promises the women that when he has finished with Jonathan they may kiss him as they please, and he throws them a bag that he has brought with him. Something inside it stirs and gives a faint cry like that of a child, and the women seize it eagerly and go away. Jonathan, sick with horror, faints, and when he wakes it is morning and he lies in his own bed, with no memory of how he came there.

Jonathan wakes in his own bed on a bright morning and finds his clothes folded neatly on a chair, though not in the way that he would have folded them himself. His watch has run down, and his boots stand in the wrong place, and every small detail proves that someone else has undressed him and put him to bed. He does not need to ask who it was, and he shivers with horror as he remembers the bag in the moonlight.

A few days later he sees the Count leave the castle dressed in Jonathan's own travelling suit, with Jonathan's three false letters in his pocket. Jonathan realises that the villagers will see the figure and take him for the English visitor, and that any crime committed in his clothes will be laid at his door. It is a clever and cruel plan, and it cuts off the last of his hopes of rescue.

That evening a woman arrives at the castle gate, wailing and beating on it with her fists, and she screams to the Count to give her back her child. Her cries ring out across the courtyard and are then drowned by the howling of wolves, as the whole pack comes rushing out of the forest at some silent command. In a few minutes every sound from the woman has ceased, and Jonathan covers his face with his hands.

Jonathan decides that he must search the Count's own rooms, and slipping through the empty castle he finds one of them unlocked, bare and covered in dust. In a corner lies a great heap of gold, with coins from Rome, Hungary, Greece and Turkey, many of them so old that their dates are worn away. There is no sign of keys or letters or any map to freedom, but in the far corner stands a heavy door that he has not seen before.

Through the heavy door he finds a winding stair, and he follows it down, step by step, into a tunnel that smells of old earth and damp stone. The air grows colder with every step, and the only light is the small glow of his candle, trembling in his unsteady hand. At the bottom the passage opens into a ruined chapel where nothing seems to have been disturbed for hundreds of years.

The chapel is full of broken tombs and heaps of rubble, but in one place the earth has been freshly dug, and many great wooden boxes stand in rows, each of them filled with black soil. Jonathan searches among them for a door or a key, and he finds neither. Then, in the biggest box, which lies half open, he sees something that makes his blood run cold.

The Count lies there on a bed of earth, as still as a dead man, with his eyes open and glassy and his skin as cold as marble, and no breath stirs his chest. Yet he looks younger than he did before, his cheeks are fuller and his lips redder, and a stain of fresh blood shows at the corner of his mouth. Jonathan has the dreadful feeling that this creature has been feeding on something terrible, and that it will not be long before it wakes.

Shaking with horror, Jonathan snatches up a spade that lies beside the box and raises it to strike the hateful face. At that moment the head turns, and the eyes fall full upon him with such burning hatred that he is paralysed, and the spade glances off, leaving only a small cut above the forehead. He turns and runs back up the stair, and he does not stop until he is in his own room, though he knows that no room in this castle is really safe.

A few days later the Szgany arrive with rough carts, and Jonathan watches from the window as they nail down the lids of the boxes and load them one by one. At last they drive away through the gate, and the clatter of the wheels dies away down the valley, so that the castle falls silent. Jonathan is now alone with the three women and the wolves, and he knows that the Count has begun his journey to England.

Jonathan knows that he cannot wait for a rescue that will never come, and that he will soon be left at the mercy of the three women. He writes a last farewell to Mina, saying that he would rather risk his life on the wall than die as a helpless prisoner. Then he climbs out of the window into the dizzy dark, and his journal ends with a single word of love.

Mina Murray, a clever and serious young woman, works as a teacher at a school in Exeter and writes many letters to her dearest friend, Lucy Westenra. In her spare time she is learning shorthand and typewriting, for she wishes to be of real use to Jonathan in his work when they are married. She has no idea, as she practises at her little desk each evening, how much those skills will matter one day.

Lucy Westenra, who is lively, pretty and rather spoiled, replies to Mina with a letter so full of excitement that her pen seems to run away from her. She declares that she has something astonishing to tell, and that she cannot possibly keep it to herself for another hour. It is, she says, that three gentlemen have asked her to marry them in a single day.

The first to speak is Dr John Seward, a young doctor with a strong, quiet face and a great reputation for cleverness, who runs a private hospital at Purfleet. Lucy likes him very much and respects him, but she does not love him, and she tells him so as gently as she can. He takes the refusal like a gentleman, though she sees how deeply it hurts him.

The second is Quincey Morris, a tall, brown American from Texas, who proposes in a rough and merry way and calls himself a poor beggar. Lucy refuses him kindly, and he answers by shaking her hand and promising that he will be her friend for as long as he lives. She is touched, and even a little ashamed that she has made so brave a man sad.

The third is Arthur Holmwood, the handsome son of a lord, and Lucy has been in love with him almost from their first meeting. When he asks her, she weeps and says yes, and then she tells Mina that she wishes a girl could marry all three men and spare everyone their pain. It is, she says, both the happiest and the saddest day of her whole life.

Dr Seward, hurt but hiding it well, buries himself in his work and records his thoughts every night on a phonograph, a machine that he has bought to keep his diary. His hospital for troubled minds stands beside an old empty house called Carfax, and his duties as its master take up most of his time. He tells himself that a busy mind has no room for sorrow, and he is only half convinced.

Among his patients he finds one who interests him above all the rest, a man named Renfield who is about fifty-nine years old, strong, polite and clever. His case is a strange one, and the doctor believes that it must have some hidden cause that he has not yet found. He studies the man with the patience of a scientist and the curiosity of a detective.

Renfield catches flies in his room and eats them, and when the flies grow scarce he gathers spiders to feed the flies and then tames sparrows to feed the spiders. He explains in a calm and reasonable voice that every life he swallows adds something to his own, and he longs to have more. Dr Seward calls him a zoophagous maniac, a life-eating madman, and writes his name at the top of a new page.

That evening, in a low and friendly mood, Quincey Morris gathers his two old friends and proposes a toast to the health of the lady they have all loved. Arthur is the happiest man in the world, and yet he is ashamed of his happiness while his friends are sad. The three of them part with warm handshakes, and promise that nothing, not even Lucy, will ever come between them.

Mina has received only a few short letters from Jonathan, and now not a single word has come for many weeks, though his last note promised a speedy return. Her anxiety grows by the day, so when Lucy and her mother invite her to stay at the seaside town of Whitby, she gladly accepts. She packs her trunk and her notebooks and tells herself that the fresh air will give her courage.

Mina steps down from the train at Whitby on a warm July afternoon and is met on the platform by Lucy and her mother, a gentle, delicate woman with a weak heart. Lucy looks lovelier than ever, with a good colour in her cheeks, and she carries Mina off in a flood of cheerful talk. They chatter all the way to the house, as friends do who have a great deal to say and little time to say it.

Whitby is a beautiful old fishing town, with red roofs that climb the hillside in rows above a harbour crowded with boats and divided by a river. High on the east cliff stand the ruins of an ancient abbey, and a long stone stair rises from the town to the church beside it. Mina decides at once that she has never seen a place so full of old stories.

In the afternoon the two friends climb the stair to the churchyard, which stands on the very edge of the cliff and looks out over the whole wide sea. Seats have been placed among the graves, and Lucy and Mina soon make one of them their own, spending long hours there with their books and their sewing. From it they can watch the ships come and go, and the smoke of the steamers drifting along the horizon.

On one of the seats they often meet an old sailor named Mr Swales, who is so ancient and weather-beaten that he looks like part of the cliff itself. He loves to talk to anyone who will listen, and he tells the girls bluntly that the gravestones around them are full of lies. Many of the stones, he says, honour men who were lost at sea and whose bodies lie nowhere near them.

Mr Swales says that he must be more than ninety years old, and he speaks of death with the calm of a man who has watched the sea take many of his friends. He laughs at the idea of a peaceful end and says that he will go when the time comes, and not a moment sooner. Mina finds him wise and rather funny, and she is sorry to say goodbye each evening.

In the evening Mina sits at the window of her room and writes in her journal, as she has done all her life, but the pages are full of her worry about Jonathan. She has heard nothing from him for weeks, and the silence presses on her like a weight, though she tries not to show it to Lucy. She tells herself that the post from Transylvania must be slow, and she does not entirely believe it.

Mrs Westenra confides to Mina that Lucy used to walk in her sleep as a child, and that the old habit sometimes returns when she is excited or upset. Mina promises to look after her friend, and she decides to lock the bedroom door each night and tie the key around her wrist. It seems a sensible precaution, and neither of them can guess how little it will help.

At breakfast a letter arrives from Arthur, and Lucy reads it three times over, blushing and smiling, before she can tell Mina what it says. His father is seriously ill, and he cannot leave London, but he sends his love and promises to come to Whitby the moment he is free. Lucy kisses the page and slips it into her pocket, where it stays for the whole of the day.

The next day is hot and strangely still, and not a breath of wind stirs the surface of the sea, which lies glassy and grey beneath a heavy sky. The old sailors in the harbour look up, mutter to one another and shake their heads, for they say that they do not like the look of it. Mina notices that even the gulls are quiet, and she feels a vague unease that she cannot explain.

As the sun sets the whole western sky turns a deep and angry red, and the fishing boats hurry back into the harbour with their sails spread. The coastguard walks along the cliff and warns the people watching that a great storm is on its way, and that they would do well to go home. Mina and Lucy linger a little longer, held by the beauty of the colours, and they do not know that something far worse than weather is coming.

That night a storm of terrible violence breaks over the coast, and the sea rises in great grey walls that smash against the harbour piers and throw spray high over the cliff. Half the town gathers on the heights in the wind, and the fishermen hold their breath and watch the horizon. Mina clings to Lucy's arm and tries to be brave, though she has never seen the sea in such a fury.

Through the rain and the flashes of lightning a schooner with every sail set comes racing toward the harbour mouth, driven by the wind like a leaf. The coastguard turns his great searchlight on her, and the crowd sees a single man standing at the wheel, who does not move or look about him. Nobody can tell how she is being steered, or why the crew do not shorten sail.

The ship sweeps past the end of the pier, and then, with a crash that makes the whole cliff tremble, she drives herself onto the sand beneath the East Cliff. Her masts shake, her sails flap in tatters, and the crowd rushes down the stairs to see what has come to them out of the storm. Mina is left almost alone on the heights, watching as the waves break over the stranded hull.

At the very moment the ship touches the shore, an enormous dog leaps from her deck onto the wet sand, shakes itself once, and races up the slope toward the cliff. It disappears over the edge of the churchyard, and neither the coastguard nor the crowd sees where it goes. Mina remembers afterward how strangely fast it ran, and how nobody tried to catch it.

A coastguard climbs aboard in the light of his lantern and finds the helmsman still at his post, but the man is dead, his hands tied to the spokes of the wheel with cords. A rosary and a small crucifix are wound tightly around his fingers, as though he had called for help and none had come. The men who see it fall silent, and the story spreads through the town before dawn.

In the dead man's pocket the men find a log, sealed in a bottle, and it tells of the voyage that ended so strangely. The schooner Demeter sailed from Varna on the Black Sea, bound for Whitby with a cargo of fifty great boxes filled with earth. The boxes were addressed to a solicitor in the town, though nobody there has any idea who sent them.

As the voyage went on, the log says, the crew became uneasy and then terrified, for men began to vanish from their posts in the night, one by one. The mate, a brave and sensible man, swore that he had seen a tall, thin stranger moving silently on the deck, who was not one of them. When the crew searched the ship from end to end they found no one.

At last the mate himself was driven mad by fear, and he sprang into the sea, leaving the captain with no one to help him. In his final lines the old man wrote that he had tied himself to the wheel with a cross in his hands, so that nothing could drag him from it. He meant to bring the ship to harbour or die in the attempt, and in a strange way he did both.

Three days later the whole town follows the captain's coffin to the churchyard on the cliff, and every boat in the harbour flies its flag. Hundreds of people who never knew the man walk in silence behind him, for they have decided that a sailor who stayed at his post to the very end deserves to be honoured as a hero. Mina, who has come with Lucy, finds herself weeping, though she cannot say exactly why.

The very next morning someone finds old Mr Swales sitting dead on his favourite seat in the churchyard, his neck broken and his face twisted in a look of terror. The people of the town shake their heads and say that he must have fallen, but nobody can explain what he was doing there in the dark. Mina is very sad, for she had grown fond of the old man, and Lucy is quiet for the rest of the day.

In the middle of the night Mina wakes with a start and sees by the light of the moon that Lucy's bed is empty and the room is cold. She throws a shawl over her nightdress and runs out into the silent streets, her heart beating wildly, for she knows how dangerous the cliff is for a sleepwalker. Behind her the sea murmurs in the dark, and above her the abbey ruins stand black against the sky.

She climbs the long stair to the churchyard in the bright moonlight, and from far away she sees the white figure of her friend sitting on the old seat. Behind Lucy, bending over her, there is a long dark shape, and Mina thinks that she sees two red points of light, like eyes, shining in the shadow. She calls out Lucy's name and runs faster, panting and stumbling up the last steps of the stair, with the wind pulling at her shawl.

When Mina reaches the seat the dark shape has vanished, and Lucy is lying back with her head thrown over the edge, breathing deeply as though asleep. On her white throat Mina sees two small red marks, and she fastens her shawl around Lucy's neck with a pin to protect her from the cold. She fears that she has pricked her friend with the pin, and she does not guess the truth.

Mina wakes Lucy gently and leads her home through the empty streets, and the next morning Lucy remembers nothing of the night, except for a strange dream of floating through a dark sea. She says that her throat feels a little sore, and Mina, who blames her own careless pin, says nothing about what she saw. The two friends spend the day quietly together, but Lucy is paler than usual.

A few days later a letter arrives from a nurse called Sister Agatha, at the hospital of Saint Joseph and Saint Mary in Budapest, and Mina tears it open with trembling hands. It tells her that Jonathan Harker arrived there some weeks before, has been very ill with a brain fever, and has begged that someone write to his fiancée. Mina reads the lines with tears in her eyes, for she has not heard his name spoken for so long.

Sister Agatha adds that the sick man raves of wolves and poison and blood, and that he calls out for Mina in the night, though when he is calm he can tell nothing of what has happened to him. Mina does not hesitate for a moment, but leaves Lucy in her mother's care, packs a small bag, and takes the first train across Europe toward Budapest. She tells herself that she will find him alive, and she repeats it again and again to the rhythm of the wheels.

At the hospital Mina follows a kind nun to a bed where a thin, pale man lies with his eyes closed, and for one terrible moment she does not know him, for he seems so much older. Then Jonathan opens his eyes and knows her, and with a cry of joy he holds out his arms. They cry together and say nothing for a long time, and the nun leaves them quietly alone.

When he is a little calmer Jonathan gives Mina his journal, which he wrote in shorthand in the castle, and he asks her never to open it unless some solemn duty forces her to. He says that he wants to forget the dreadful things he has seen, or to believe that they were only a sick man's visions. Mina ties the little book with a ribbon, seals it with wax, and promises to guard it with her life.

A few days later, in the hospital chapel, a priest marries them, with Sister Agatha as a witness, and Jonathan holds his bride's hand with a happy, shaking grip. Mina is not ashamed of the plain white room or the hospital walls, for she feels that she has never been so rich. She is proud to be his wife and swears that she will stand beside him in sickness and in health.

Soon afterwards they take the long journey home to England, and in Exeter old Mr Hawkins welcomes them as warmly as if they were his own children. Slowly Jonathan grows stronger in the quiet house, and Mina watches over him with a mixture of joy and worry. Yet he often wakes in the night with a cry, and she holds his hand until he sleeps again.

Lucy returns to London with her mother and settles into their house at Hillingham, but the weeks by the sea do not seem to have done her any good, and she sleeps very badly. At night she hears a great bat beating its wings against the window of her room, and each morning she wakes more tired than when she went to bed. Her mother, who is ill herself, does not notice how pale her daughter has become.

Arthur is anxious about his sweetheart, but he cannot leave his father, who lies seriously ill, and so he writes a short, urgent letter to his friend Dr Seward. He begs him to see Lucy and to tell him the whole truth about her health, however bad it may be. Seward, who has not forgotten his own feelings, agrees at once, for he would do anything for his friend's sake.

Seward finds Lucy as pretty and as cheerful as ever, but when he examines her he is shocked to see how thin and bloodless she has become. Her gums are white, her pulse is weak, and yet he can find no sign of any illness that would explain it. He goes home puzzled and uneasy, and he suspects that this is a case beyond his own knowledge.

He remembers his old master, Professor Abraham Van Helsing of Amsterdam, a man of vast learning who knows more about strange diseases than anyone in Europe, and he sends a telegram begging him to come. The reply arrives at once, and the professor takes the next boat across the sea. Seward feels a great weight lift from his mind, though he cannot tell why he should.

Van Helsing proves to be a short, broad-shouldered man with a strong face, a shock of grey hair and kind, clever eyes that miss nothing. He examines Lucy in silence for a long time, and when he sees the two small marks on her throat his face grows deadly serious. Outside the room he tells Seward that her blood must be replaced at once, or she will die.

That evening Arthur arrives, and Van Helsing explains that a transfusion is needed, which means that healthy blood must be passed from one person into another. Arthur gladly lies down beside Lucy and offers his arm, and soon the colour begins to creep back into her white cheeks. Van Helsing watches the change and nods with relief, but he does not smile.

The professor also brings a great bundle of garlic flowers, which he rubs round the window and the door and then twists into a wreath for Lucy's neck. She laughs at the strong smell and at the strange medicine, but Van Helsing tells her very seriously that she must never take it off. Lucy, who trusts the old man, promises to obey, though her mother thinks it very queer.

The next night Seward gives his own blood, while Van Helsing sits beside the bed with a watch in his hand and counts the minutes. In the morning Lucy is a little stronger and has a little more colour, but the two doctors can see that the improvement is slow. They know that she is losing blood faster than they can give it back.

On the third night Van Helsing himself gives some of his blood, though he looks tired and old, and for the first time Lucy sleeps without a single bad dream. By the morning she smiles and eats a good breakfast, and Seward begins to hope. Yet the professor does not smile, and he keeps the garlic flowers fresh around her with great care.

Then Quincey Morris arrives and offers his blood, saying that he is only too glad to help a lady whom he has always loved as a friend. He lies down in his turn, and Lucy sleeps peacefully beside him, her hand in his, while the three men watch over her. For the first time in days the room seems full of hope, and no one thinks about the dark window behind the curtain.

Van Helsing is called home to Amsterdam for a few days, and before he goes he gives Seward strict orders to guard Lucy day and night. The windows must stay shut, the garlic flowers must be kept fresh, and Lucy must never be left alone in the dark. Seward promises to obey every word, though he does not understand why the professor is so serious.

Lucy's mother, a kind and gentle woman who knows nothing of the danger, finds the smell of garlic dreadful and believes that her daughter needs fresh air. She quietly takes the flowers from the room and opens the window wide, and Lucy, too weak to protest, does not stop her. By the evening she is paler than she has been for days, and her breathing is shallow and quick.

Seward, exhausted by many sleepless nights, decides to go home to his hospital for a single night of rest, leaving Lucy with her mother. A telegram from Van Helsing, begging him not to leave her for an hour, reaches him far too late. It is the only night of the whole illness that he is not at her side, and he will blame himself for it for a long time.

That night Lucy and her mother lie side by side in the big bed, and the house is very still. Lucy hears the flapping of great wings at the window, and somewhere beyond the garden the long cry of a wolf rises into the dark. She cannot say why, but she feels more afraid than she has ever been in her life.

Without warning a huge grey wolf thrusts its head against the glass, and the window breaks with a crash, scattering fragments across the floor. The animal, which has escaped from the zoo, stands in the broken frame with burning eyes, and a cold wind blows out the candle and sets the curtains flying. Lucy tries to scream, but she is too weak and too frightened, and no sound will come from her throat.

Lucy's mother raises herself on one elbow, sees the animal, and gives a terrible cry, for her weak heart cannot bear the shock. She falls back across the bed, and in her fall the wreath of garlic is torn away from Lucy's neck and flung aside. She is dead before the wolf has gone, and there is nothing that her frightened daughter can do.

Lucy lies helpless beneath the weight of her dead mother, too weak to move and too frightened to think. She calls for the servants again and again, but they lie in a deep, unnatural sleep and do not hear her. At last her voice fails, and she lies still, listening to the wind in the broken window.

In the morning Seward comes and is horrified to find the shattered window, the servants asleep in their beds and Lucy lying cold and white beside her dead mother. He sends a telegram at once, and Van Helsing hurries from the station, takes one look at the room and orders that the garlic be hung once more around the window and the door. They must save her if they can, he says, and she must never again be left alone.

Arthur arrives, pale with grief for Lucy's mother, and he sits beside Lucy and takes her hand. She looks at him with strange, bright eyes and a changed, dreamy voice, and she asks him to kiss her. Van Helsing seizes him by the shoulders and drags him back with a cry, for he has seen something in her face that fills him with fear.

That night Lucy dies, and as her breathing stops, the dreadful marks fade, and her face grows soft and sweet and beautiful once more. Arthur kisses her for the last time, and Van Helsing watches them with a grave and troubled look, for he knows that this may not be the end. Outside, the wind has dropped, and the morning that comes through the window is cold, still and grey.

On a grey and windy day Lucy is buried in her family's tomb at Kingstead, beside her mother, and Arthur weeps openly as the coffin is carried into the vault. Van Helsing stands a little apart from the mourners, watching the tomb with a sad and anxious face, as if he expected it to be disturbed. He does not say what he fears, and Seward is too tired and sorrowful to ask.

A few days later the newspapers begin to tell a strange story about small children who have been found wandering on the heath after dark, weak and pale, with two small wounds on their throats. The children all say that a beautiful lady took them away, and they call her the bloofer lady, in their own baby language. Seward reads the reports with a growing chill, and he remembers the marks that he saw on Lucy.

Van Helsing takes Seward to see one of the children in hospital, and the doctor sees at once that its tiny wounds are just like the marks on Lucy's neck. The professor then tells him, in a quiet and serious voice, that there are things in the world which most people refuse to believe, and that some of the dead do not lie quietly in their graves. Seward listens in disbelief, but he cannot find a single argument to answer him.

At night the two men go to the churchyard at Kingstead, force open the door of the vault with Van Helsing's tools, and lift the lid of Lucy's coffin. Seward expects to see his dead friend, but the coffin is empty, and he nearly drops his lantern in terror. Van Helsing says calmly that he was right, and that they must hide and wait.

They hide among the dark yew trees until after midnight, when a white figure comes gliding across the grass toward the tomb, carrying something in its arms. As it passes through a patch of moonlight, they see that the burden is a small child, and that the figure is a woman in a long white dress. Seward's heart almost stops, for he knows the walk and the shape of the head, though the face is hidden.

Van Helsing opens his lantern, and the light falls upon Lucy's face, which is no longer sweet but cruel and hungry, with red stains on the lips and teeth that are long and sharp. She throws the child down like a doll and hisses at the two men, but when the professor holds up a golden cross she cannot come near him. With a last angry look she slips away into the shadows, and the men lift the frightened child and carry it to safety.

The next day Van Helsing tells Arthur and Quincey the truth, and Arthur is so shocked and angry that he nearly strikes the old man, who has spoken against the girl he loved. Then he sees the deep sorrow in the professor's face, and he agrees to come to the churchyard that night and judge for himself. Quincey, who has seen strange things in his travels, listens without a word and nods.

That night the four men enter the vault with lanterns and lift the lid of the coffin, and there lies Lucy, more beautiful than she ever was in life, with rosy cheeks and red lips. Arthur stares at her in horror and love, for he cannot understand how the dead can look so alive. Then he sees her long, sharp teeth shining between her red lips, and he turns away from the coffin with a groan.

Van Helsing explains gently that the only way to free Lucy's soul from her dreadful state is to drive a wooden stake through her heart, and that it will bring her peace at last. Arthur is as pale as the dead, but he says that he will do it himself, because he loved her and will not let another man do it. The old professor puts the stake and the hammer into his hands and tells him what to do.

Arthur sets the point above her heart and strikes with all his strength, while Van Helsing reads the prayers for the dead in a deep and solemn voice. The body shudders once, and then a great stillness comes over the face, which grows calm, sweet and sad, as it was in life. The four men close the tomb and walk away in the dawn, and Van Helsing tells them that the work is only half done, because the one who made her is still free.

Old Mr Hawkins dies suddenly after a short illness, and he leaves all his fortune and his house to Jonathan and Mina, whom he loved like his own children. They mourn him sincerely and deeply, for he was their kind guide and friend through every difficult year of their lives. Jonathan, who has been recovering slowly, is moved to tears and does not know how to thank a dead man.

After the funeral they move to London, where Jonathan takes up his work again and grows a little stronger every week. On a bright afternoon they walk along Piccadilly, arm in arm, looking in the shop windows and talking of ordinary things like any happy young couple. For a few hours the dark memory of the castle seems very far away.

Suddenly Jonathan stops dead in the middle of the pavement, and his face turns as white as paper. Across the street a tall, thin man with a hooked nose, a black moustache and a pointed beard is staring with burning eyes at a pretty girl who is getting into a carriage. There is something in his cold, hungry gaze that makes Mina shiver, though she cannot say why.

Jonathan whispers that the man is the Count, and that he has grown young again, and he grips her arm so tightly that it hurts. At that moment the stranger turns and looks straight at him, and his face hardens with a look of such hatred that Jonathan almost falls. Then he steps into a cab and is carried away, and Jonathan, shaking from head to foot, can hardly stand.

Mina leads her husband to a quiet tea shop and gives him strong tea until the colour returns to his face, but he can hardly speak. That night, while he lies in an exhausted sleep, she decides that the solemn duty he spoke of in Budapest has come at last. She takes his journal from its hiding place, breaks the wax seal, and begins to read.

She reads through the night by the light of a small lamp, her heart growing colder with every page, as the castle, the Count and the three women rise from the shorthand lines. At last she understands that the story is no sick man's dream, and that a monster who feeds on the blood of the living is walking the streets of London. She sits quite still as the dawn grows grey, and she feels that she has aged ten years.

In the morning she tells Jonathan quietly that she has read his journal from beginning to end, and that she believes every word of it. He bursts into tears, for he has lived for weeks in terror that he was mad, and her belief is like water to a man dying of thirst. They hold each other for a long time, and then they begin to plan what to do.

Mina has already written to Dr Seward to ask for news of her friend Lucy's last illness, and now a telegram comes in reply, to say that Professor Van Helsing, who nursed Lucy, wishes to meet her. The professor will arrive by an early train the next morning, and he asks that both of them be at home to receive him. Mina cannot imagine why the news makes her so nervous, but she prepares the best tea she can.

The next morning a short, broad man with grey hair and kind eyes steps into the room, takes Mina's hands in his and thanks her for her kindness to poor Lucy. She gives him her own diary and Jonathan's journal, which she has copied out on her typewriter, and he settles down to read, asking only for a quiet corner. Hour after hour he reads, and Mina watches his face change from interest to amazement and at last to hope.

At last the professor rises, his eyes shining, and tells Jonathan that his story is the missing piece which explains everything that has happened to poor Lucy. He praises the courage of the young couple and says that, with their help, there is a chance to destroy the monster. He invites them to come to Dr Seward's hospital at Purfleet and join the little band of friends who are ready to fight.

Jonathan and Mina take the train to Purfleet and walk up to Dr Seward's hospital, a large, grey, many-windowed house surrounded by a high wall and green lawns. Jonathan looks past the garden and sees, beyond a second wall, the old chimneys and broken roof of a house that he recognises at once, since it is Carfax. He realises with a shiver that the Count has chosen to live beside a house of troubled minds.

Dr Seward keeps his diary on a phonograph, and when Mina offers to type it out for the others, he gives her the wax cylinders with gratitude. As she listens to his tired, loving voice describing Lucy's last weeks, she learns what happened in the sickroom, and she cries for her dear friend. Her skill at the typewriter turns out to be the greatest help that she could give.

That evening Arthur, who is now Lord Godalming, and Quincey Morris arrive at the hospital, and the whole company gathers in the doctor's study with Mina's neat typed pages laid out before them. They have all read the story, and not a single one of them laughs, for each has seen enough to know that it is true. Mina sits among them, a quiet young woman with a notebook, and they all treat her with the greatest respect.

Van Helsing rises and tells them gravely that Count Dracula is a vampire, one of the undead, who has lived for centuries by drinking the blood of the living. He is as strong as twenty men, he commands wolves, rats and bats, he can bring on fog and storms, and he can change his shape. Yet he is also a clever and ancient enemy, and they must not underestimate him.

But the vampire has weaknesses, the professor continues, and the friends must learn to use them. He fears garlic, holy symbols and sacred things, he casts no reflection in a mirror, he cannot enter a house unless somebody invites him in, and in the daylight most of his powers fail him. Above all, he must rest each day in the earth of his own country, and without it he grows weak.

Van Helsing's plan is simple and bold: if the Count has brought boxes of earth from his own land, the friends must find every one and make it unfit for him with holy bread. When no safe resting place is left to him, he will be driven out into the open, where they can destroy him. The others listen in silence, and each of them knows that the danger will be great.

Jonathan tells them what he knows, for he helped to buy Carfax, and he explains that fifty boxes of earth came by ship to Whitby and were taken by train and by wagon to the old house. If they were all put in the chapel there, it should be easy enough to find them. But he adds that the Count is cunning, and that he may have other houses in London.

Dr Seward leads them to an upper window, from which they can see Carfax standing alone behind its high stone wall, with its blind windows and its crooked chimneys. It is only a short walk from his own hospital, and the thought that the Count has been living so near his patients fills him with dismay. Quincey, who has been quiet, says that he would like to see the inside of the place as soon as possible.

Mina asks to meet some of the patients, and Seward takes her to see Renfield, who is calm and polite and bows to her like a gentleman of the old school. She is struck by his pale, sad face and by the clear sense that he is speaking from a world far away. When she leaves, she is thoughtful, and she says that he seems more like a man in chains than a madman.

Later Renfield begs Dr Seward to let him go, promising that he will be good and harmless if only he is free, and he even says that his soul is in danger. Seward, who cannot forget the patient's strange habits and sudden rages, is gentle but firm, and he refuses. Renfield sits down on his bed with a bitter look and mutters that the doctor will be sorry.

When darkness falls, the five men set out for Carfax, armed with lanterns, a bunch of keys, and a bag of holy things that Van Helsing has gathered for the night. Mina stays at the hospital, and she watches the little lights move across the lawn until the trees swallow them up. She tells herself bravely that she is not afraid, though her hands tremble on the windowsill.

Jonathan, who has the keys, unlocks the old front door, and it swings open with a long groan of rusty hinges. A thick smell of damp earth and age drifts out of the darkness, and the friends cover their faces with their handkerchiefs. Van Helsing steps forward first with his lantern raised, and the others follow close behind him.

Inside, the rooms are filled with dust, and thick curtains of spider webs hang from the ceilings like grey lace. The lanterns throw long, wavering shadows over the walls, and their footsteps sound very loud in the empty halls. The men move from room to room in silence, and every creak of the old boards makes them start.

At last they reach the old chapel, where they find great wooden boxes standing in rows, each filled with fresh earth that smells of a far country. They count them one by one, and the total is twenty-nine, though the Count brought fifty to England. Twenty-one boxes, then, are hidden somewhere else in London, and the thought troubles every one of the friends.

Suddenly the floor seems to come alive, and hundreds of rats pour into the chapel from every crack and corner, their eyes shining like tiny sparks in the lantern light. They are larger than any rats the men have ever seen, and they crowd closer and closer until a living grey carpet covers the stones. Even brave Quincey takes a step backward, and Seward grips his lantern with both hands.

Arthur puts two fingers to his lips and whistles loudly, and several small terrier dogs come bounding in from the passage where he left them. The rats scream and scatter in every direction, and in a few moments the chapel is empty, with only a few of them lying on the floor. The dogs stand panting by Arthur's side, wagging their tails, and he strokes them proudly and thanks them for their help.

Van Helsing takes from his bag a small box that holds pieces of consecrated bread, and he lays one piece inside each of the twenty-nine boxes while he prays in a low voice. He explains that the earth has now been made holy, and that the Count can never again rest in it. One by one the boxes are cleansed of his power, and the friends feel the dread in the chapel slowly lift.

In the study Jonathan finds a heap of keys, each with a label attached, and a bundle of deeds and papers that prove the Count has bought other houses in London. Three of them are named in the papers, in Piccadilly, in Mile End and in Bermondsey, and the friends write down every address with care. It is clear that the Count has prepared his hiding places as carefully as a general plans a war.

The next morning Jonathan visits the office of the carriers who brought the boxes from Whitby, and a helpful clerk searches the old books for him. He learns that the boxes which are not at Carfax were delivered to the three houses named in the deeds, and he returns with the numbers and the dates. Van Helsing is delighted, and says that they will visit each house in turn.

That evening the men agree among themselves that Mina must not be taken into danger again, for the work ahead is too perilous, and she must be protected. Mina, who has proved her courage a hundred times, accepts their decision with a heavy heart, and she goes back to her typewriter and her worries. None of them yet knows that the greatest danger will come to her at the hospital, in the quiet of her own room.

One evening an attendant leaves a door open, and Renfield, who has been calm for days, suddenly bolts out of the hospital and across the lawn toward the wall of Carfax. Dr Seward, who sees him from a window, hurries after him with two strong nurses, though the patient moves with surprising speed. The moon is hidden behind thick clouds, and the garden is full of moving shadows.

They find him at last standing at the window of the old chapel at Carfax, with his face pressed close to the glass and his lips moving as if in conversation with someone inside. Seward, listening, can hear him speak to his master in a humble, eager voice, promising to do whatever he is told, though no other voice answers. The sight chills him far more than any of the man's wild rages, because it seems to him a madness with a purpose.

As the nurses lay their hands on him, a huge bat flies silently over their heads from the direction of the house and vanishes into the night. Renfield cries out in a strange, joyful voice that he is the master's servant, and for a moment he struggles with the strength of three men. Then his strength suddenly fails, and the nurses are able to take him back across the lawn to the hospital.

In his room Renfield becomes quiet and sad, and no questions can draw from him a word about what he saw or why he ran. Seward writes in his diary that he does not understand his patient, and that he is more disturbed by the man's silence than by his earlier fits. He decides that someone must keep watch on him every night, and that he will do so himself when he can.

At the same time Mina begins to feel strangely tired in the mornings, and she notices that both she and Jonathan are sleeping far more deeply than they have ever done before. She tells herself that it is only the strain of the last few weeks, but she cannot shake off a heavy weakness that is growing day by day. Her cheeks are paler than they should be, and she is too proud and too anxious to tell anybody.

One night Mina dreams that a white mist is creeping under the door and across the floor of her room, thickening until it fills the air like smoke. In the heart of the mist she sees two red eyes shining, and a tall, dark shape that bends over her, though she cannot move a finger or cry out. In the morning she remembers it only as a bad dream and says nothing.

In the daytime Renfield is calm and even cheerful, and Seward is astonished by the change, since he has not seen the patient so rational since he came. Then Renfield begs him earnestly to send him to some other place far from Purfleet, and he says that his life depends on it. The doctor, who still does not trust him, refuses, and the smile slowly fades from the patient's face.

In the middle of that night Seward is woken by a cry from Renfield's room, followed by a heavy fall, and he runs along the passage with a lamp in his hand. He finds the patient lying on the floor of his cell, badly hurt, with blood on his face and one arm bent beneath him. The doctor kneels at once, and the others, who have heard the noise, come running to the door.

With his last strength Renfield whispers that the master came to his window and promised him many lives, but that he would not stand by while he took the life of the lady. He says that he tried to stop him, and that the master threw him down, and that he has gone to Mrs Harker's room. His eyes close, and he is dead before Seward can find a single word to answer him.

Seward, Van Helsing, Arthur and Quincey tear along the corridor toward the room where Jonathan and Mina are sleeping, their hearts pounding with fear. The door is locked fast from inside, and no sound comes from behind it, and Quincey throws himself against it with all his weight. At the third blow the lock breaks, and the door bursts inward with a crash that echoes through the sleeping house.

The door bursts open, and by the pale moonlight the friends see a sight that none of them will ever forget. Jonathan lies on the bed with his face turned toward the wall, breathing like a drugged man, while Mina kneels at the bedside in her white nightdress. Beside her stands a tall, thin figure in black, holding her wrists in one hand and pressing her face against his chest, which is stained with blood, with the other.

The Count turns upon the intruders with his face distorted by fury and his red eyes blazing, and he seems about to spring. But Van Helsing steps boldly forward, holding up the holy bread in one hand and a crucifix in the other, and the Count falls back before them. A cloud covers the moon, and when the lamp is lit again the figure has vanished, and only a thin white mist is curling out beneath the door.

Mina rises slowly from the floor with blood on her lips and her white nightdress, and she cries out in a terrible voice that she is unclean. Van Helsing, moved to the depths of his heart, touches her forehead gently with the holy bread, and it burns into her skin and leaves a scar as red as fire. She hides her face in her hands and begs them not to look at her.

Jonathan wakes at last from his unnatural sleep, and when he sees the blood and his wife's white face he cries out in anguish. In the grey light of morning the others see that his hair, which was brown only a few weeks before, has turned white. Mina holds his hand tightly and tells him that she loves him and that he must not blame himself for what has happened.

Mina, though she is weak and shaking, insists on telling the friends everything that has happened, because she knows that every detail may help them. She says that the Count came to her room in a white mist and forced her to drink his blood. He told her that she would soon be one of his own and would help him against her friends, and the listeners sit in silence, their faces white with horror and pity.

Then Mina asks her friends for a solemn promise: if the day comes when she changes into a vampire like Lucy, they must free her, even though they love her. Van Helsing gives his word at once, and one by one the others do the same, with tears running down their faces. Jonathan is the last, and he swears it in a whisper, with his face buried in his wife's hair.

Van Helsing explains that the Count has joined Mina to himself, and that for good or ill she will now sometimes feel his thoughts and know where he is. This is a danger, for he may learn what she knows, but it is also their greatest chance of following him wherever he goes. The professor says that he will try to use the link, and Mina agrees bravely.

After the long night the men make a promise of their own, which is that there shall be no more secrets from Mina, and that she will be treated as one of the band. She thanks them in a quiet voice and says that she is stronger than they think and that she will do all that she can. For the first time since the attack, a little colour returns to her cheeks.

The next morning the friends travel to Piccadilly, taking with them the keys, the holy bread and their courage, and Jonathan leads them to the big empty house that the Count has bought. He opens the front door with his key, and a smell of old earth meets them in the dusty hall, like a breath from the grave. Van Helsing says in a low voice that this is the right house, and that they must be quick.

In a dusty room at the back of the house the friends find the Count's boxes of earth, standing in a row, just like those at Carfax. They have only begun to treat them with the holy bread when they hear a key turn in the front door, and the sound echoes through the empty rooms. Every man freezes, and Jonathan, who is nearest the passage, feels for the long knife that he has brought with him.

The key turns, the door opens, and Count Dracula himself steps calmly into the hall, as if he were returning to his own house, which in a sense he is. For a moment he stands quite still, looking from one face to another with his cold eyes, and a faint smile touches his lips. Then Jonathan, who has not forgotten the castle, springs at him with the long curved knife, and the Count leaps aside.

The blade whistles through the air and cuts the Count's coat from the shoulder to the hip, missing the man by a hair's breadth. A heap of gold coins and banknotes spills from the torn pocket and rings on the floor, spinning and shining in the light of the window. The Count's face turns white with rage, and for a moment he looks less like a man than a cornered wolf.

Then he throws himself through the window with a crash, and the glass flies in all directions as he falls to the paved yard below. He stands up among the broken pieces, unhurt, and looks back at the friends with a smile of terrible mockery. They rush to the window and look down at him, but none of them dares to follow him into the yard.

In a voice that carries clearly through the broken window the Count tells them that they have not left him without a place to rest, for he has many others, and that his revenge has only begun. He says that he has spread it over centuries, that time is on his side, and that the women whom they love are already his. Then he turns and vanishes into the stable behind the house, and the friends are left in silence.

The friends gather the gold and the papers from the floor, and then, without wasting a moment, they separate to visit the other houses at Mile End and Bermondsey. In each of them they find the boxes of earth waiting in a cellar or a shed, and Van Helsing's holy bread is laid in every one. By nightfall the Count's hiding places in London have been destroyed, all but one.

At sunrise Van Helsing sits Mina in a chair and, with a slow movement of his hand, sends her into a deep sleep in which she can speak what she senses. In a faraway voice she says that she hears water lapping, wood creaking and the wind in ropes, and that the world around her is utterly dark. Her answers are hesitant, but the professor listens with the closest attention and does not interrupt.

From the sounds Van Helsing understands that the Count lies in his box in the hold of a ship, and that he is leaving England for ever. It is both a danger and a relief, for the monster is gone from London, but he is returning to a place where he is stronger than anywhere else. The friends sit together in the study and talk long into the night about what to do.
