At the docks the friends make careful inquiries and learn that only one ship has left on the evening tide for the Black Sea, a vessel called the Czarina Catherine, bound for Varna. The clerk remembers that a single large box was carried aboard at the last moment by a strange, silent man whom nobody could describe. Jonathan, listening with his heart beating fast, feels sure that this is the very box that they are searching for.

Van Helsing says that the Count is going home to his castle in the mountains, where he is safe and where his power is greatest. The friends decide that they must follow him, reach his country before he does, and destroy him there once and for all. It is a bold plan, and everyone knows that not all of them may come back.

Mina declares that she will not be left behind, for she is the only one who can feel where the Count is, and the men, remembering their promise, agree at last. That same evening the whole company sets off by train for Varna, with their luggage, their weapons and a heavy box of holy things. As the lights of London slip away behind them, Mina holds her husband's hand and looks bravely ahead.

The friends cross Europe by the fastest trains, changing carriages and platforms with scarcely a pause, and reach Varna on the Black Sea at last. They take rooms in a hotel near the harbour and make inquiries about the Czarina Catherine, but nobody has seen her. Every day that the ship fails to appear, the waiting grows harder to bear.

Each morning at sunrise and each evening at sunset, Van Helsing puts Mina into a trance so that she may tell him what she senses. She says that she hears the same lapping of water and creaking of wood as before, and that the ship is moving, though the harbour remains empty. Her answers are faint and strange, and she is always exhausted when she wakes.

At last a telegram arrives to say that the Czarina Catherine has been sent on to Galatz, a river port on the Danube, instead of coming to Varna. Van Helsing realises at once that the Count has changed his plan, and that his servants have been working to help him. The friends hurry back to the station and catch the first train to Galatz.

At Galatz they find the Czarina Catherine lying in the harbour, and her captain tells them a puzzling tale of a thick fog that followed his ship across half the world, though the weather around it was clear. He says that as soon as the ship was tied up, a man came and took away a large box, saying that it belonged to a merchant in the town. The captain did not like the box, and he was glad to see the last of it.

The man who took the box was an agent of the Count, and he handed it to a band of Slovak carters, who loaded it on a boat and took it up the river Sereth that same night. When the friends visit the agent, he cannot tell them where it will go, only that the boat is headed toward the mountains. Van Helsing, studying the map, says that the Count must be heading for his castle.

Van Helsing decides that the friends must divide into three parties, for the Count may leave the river at any place and take to the road. He and Mina will go by road toward the Borgo Pass and the castle, and the others will follow the boat by water and by land. Mina, who feels the Count's presence in her blood, agrees that this is the only way.

Jonathan and Arthur hire a swift steam launch and chase the boat up the river Sereth, pushing the little engine as hard as it will go. They stop at every village to ask the boatmen what they have seen, and the answers always point onward. Jonathan thinks of his wife on the road, and he urges the helmsman to go faster.

Quincey and Seward buy strong horses and ride along the bank of the river, so that if the boat turns toward the shore they will be there to meet it. They carry rifles and plenty of supplies, and they keep a careful watch on the water and the road ahead. Quincey, who grew up on the plains of Texas, feels the old, familiar joy of the chase.

Van Helsing and Mina travel by carriage on rough roads that climb into the mountains toward the Borgo Pass, with the sun low and the air growing colder. Mina, in a trance, says that she can hear lowing cattle, creaking wheels and men's voices, and that the Count is on the move at last. The professor writes down every word that she says, and he urges the driver on through the gathering cold.

At dusk Van Helsing builds a fire and draws a wide circle around it with crumbs of holy bread, and Mina sits inside it, wrapped in her furs. In the dark three pale women come out of the mist, beautiful and terrible, and they call softly to her, but they cannot cross the line. The horses scream, wolves howl in the mountains, and Van Helsing stands guard beside Mina with a cross in his hand.

At dawn, when the pale women have vanished with the mist, Van Helsing tells Mina to stay inside the circle, which no evil can enter, and sets out alone for the castle. He climbs the snowy path to the gloomy chapel, and there he finds three tombs in which the women lie as if asleep, lovely and cold. With prayers and great sorrow he frees them, and the three bodies crumble into dust and are at peace.

In the Count's own chapel Van Helsing finds a great tomb marked with a single name, and he lays a piece of holy bread inside it so that the Count can never lie there again. He then fills the doorway of the castle with the same holy bread, so that nothing evil can pass in or out. His work done, he walks back down the mountain in the cold light, tired and grey but unafraid.

That afternoon the friends close in from three sides on the mountain road, for Mina says that the Count is very near. Soon a cart appears in the distance, drawn by fast horses and carrying a great box, while armed men ride all around it and urge it toward the castle. The sun is already sinking toward the peaks, and the friends know that they have only minutes.

Jonathan and Quincey leap onto the cart and fight their way through the guards to the great box, while Arthur and Seward ride up behind them. As the sun touches the mountains, Jonathan slashes his long knife through the Count's throat, and Quincey drives his own blade into his heart. The Count's body crumbles into dust before their eyes, and on his face there is a look of peace.

In the struggle Quincey has been wounded, and he sinks to the ground, where his friends gather around him as the gypsies flee. He tells them with a smile that he is glad to have helped, and when he sees that Mina's forehead is as white as the snow, he gives thanks that the curse has passed away. With a gentle sigh he dies, and those who loved him kneel beside him in silence.

The friends leave the castle and the mountains with heavy hearts, grieving for the brave American but thankful that the monster is gone for ever. Mina walks between her husband and the old professor, and her face, no longer scarred, is peaceful for the first time in many months. Behind them the castle stands in the morning light, empty and silent, a ruin and nothing more.

Back in England the survivors rebuild their lives, and the memory of their adventure grows quiet. Arthur and Dr Seward both marry happily, and Jonathan and Mina live in peace, though they never forget the friend who gave his life for them. Sometimes at night Jonathan still wakes with a start, but Mina is there with her hand in his.

Seven years pass, and Jonathan and Mina have a little son, whose birthday falls on the very day when Quincey Morris died. Mina holds a secret belief that some of the brave American's spirit has passed into the child, and they give him a long string of names that join all their friends together. In daily life, however, they call him simply Quincey, and he is a cheerful, brave and curious little boy.

In the summer of that year the family makes a journey to Transylvania and walks over the old ground, from the Borgo Pass to the road where Quincey fell. It is hard to believe that what they saw with their own eyes and heard with their own ears was true, for every trace of it has been blotted out. The castle stands where it always did, high above a waste of desolation, and the wind in the pines is the only voice.

Back at home Jonathan takes the old papers from the safe and sees that they are nothing but typewriting, with hardly one real document among them. Nobody could be asked to believe so wild a story on such evidence, yet Van Helsing, with the little boy on his knee, says that they want no proofs. One day, he says, the boy will understand how brave a woman his mother is, and how some men loved her so well that they dared much for her sake.
